# Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning

Dixi Yao⁰⁰footnotemark: 0 ²²footnotemark: 2 ^(†)^(†)thanks:
Correspondence to: Dixi Yao \$¡\$dixi@uchicago.edu\$¿\$    Tahseen
Rabbani²²footnotemark: 2    Manzil Zaheer³³footnotemark: 3    Tian Li
²²footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: ²²footnotemark: 2 University of Chicago
   ³³footnotemark: 3   Google DeepMind

###### Abstract

We propose a federated learning-like framework, _Federation over Text_
(FoT), that enables multiple clients solving different tasks to
collectively generate a shared library of metacognitive insights by
iteratively federating their local reasoning processes without sharing
actual problem instances or task instructions. Instead of federation
over gradients (e.g., as in distributed training), FoT operates at the
semantic level without any gradient optimization or supervision signal.
Iteratively, each client runs an LLM agent that does local thinking and
self-improvement on their specific tasks independently, and shares
reasoning traces with a central server, which aggregates and distills
them into a cross-task (and cross-domain) insight library that existing
and future agents can leverage to improve performance on related tasks.
Experiments show that FoT improves reasoning effectiveness and
efficiency across a wide range of challenging applications, including
mathematical problem solving, cross-domain collaboration, real-world
daily tasks, and machine learning research insight discovery.
Specifically, it improves average performance scores by 25% while
reducing the reasoning tokens by 4% across the first three applications.
In the research insight discovery application, FoT is able to generate
insights that cover over 80% of the major contributions in the
subsequent papers.

## 1 Introduction

LLM-powered agents are increasingly deployed for complex, multi-step
tasks \[[39](#bib.bib27), [16](#bib.bib25), [19](#bib.bib52),
[27](#bib.bib19), [40](#bib.bib6), [47](#bib.bib21), e.g.,\]. However,
they can suffer from two major limitations. First, reasoning can be
inefficient: agents often reason from scratch given an input instance,
repeatedly solving similar problems, which can be computationally
expensive and slow. Second, reasoning in multi-agent systems typically
occurs in an isolated manner, where agents are chained by passing
prompts or intermediate outputs \[[11](#bib.bib1), e.g.,\]. While agents
exchange task solutions within a session, their internal thinking
processes and full reasoning histories are not explicitly stored or
communicated. As a result, these hard-won thinking processes are lost
and cannot be reused or shared across agents.

It remains underexplored how to automatically transfer, reuse, or
distill independent reasoning traces to help guide and improve future
reasoning processes for similar agents or across domains. At the same
time, classical distributed or federated paradigms for knowledge
sharing \[[21](#bib.bib3)\] may not be suitable for learning
generalizable insights from agents’ reasoning traces. Averaging the
gradients or weights of entire (or part of) large generative models can
be computationally prohibitive, impossible for closed-source LLMs, and
more importantly, not interpretable as parameter aggregation is not
explicitly equivalent to sharing abstract, high-level reasoning
summaries.

To this end, we propose _federation over text_ (FoT), a federated-like
framework that enables a set of agents to collaboratively and
iteratively build a shared, evolving library of reusable insights from
independent local reasoning traces (expressed in natural language)
without communicating actual problem instances. Unlike traditional
multi-agent systems that decompose a single complex task into subtasks,
FoT operates across multiple independent agents over diverse but related
tasks. Each agent solves some task with a base language model, and our
goal is to generate an insight library—a high-level aggregation of the
common principles and ideas shared across the agents’ tasks.

Unlike traditional distributed learning, which averages gradients or
model updates in a high-dimensional, uninterpretable space, FoT operates
at the semantic, text level without any parameter optimization,
fine-tuning, or reinforcement learning. In particular, at each round,
agents transmit concise metacognitive summaries of their problem-solving
processes to a central server (which can be physical or logically
virtual). The server, acting as an aggregator, identifies and distills
recurring reasoning fragments from these summaries into new, explicit
insights and sends the insight library back to the agents for the next
round. We note that FoT is a general framework that allows each agent to
use any local reasoning model combined with any local self-improvement
workflows for their individual tasks, as long as summarized reasoning
traces are shared at each iteration. Meanwhile, we note that our
proposed FoT approach is analogous to the classic federated/distributed
learning setting, where these two regimes can be interpreted within the
same conceptual framework (side-by-side comparisons in
[Table 1](#S3.T1 "In 3.1 Analogies Between Federated/Distributed Learning and FoT ‣ 3 Federation over Text ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")).
Additionally, FoT offers similar benefits as FL in that only abstracted
reasoning traces are shared instead of raw problem instances. But
operating in the semantic text space as in FoT provides more
interpretable control on what information is transmitted, and allows us
to identify and block sensitive information more easily.

We apply FoT to various applications including mathematical problem
solving, multi-domain collaboration (scientific question-answering,
coding, and Humanity’s Last Exam), real-world daily tasks, and research
insight discovery
(Section [4](#S4 "4 Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")).
We compare our framework with a range of baselines, such as isolated
reasoning without collaboration and other forms of cross-agent knowledge
sharing. Across the first three applications with previous benchmarks,
FoT improves the accuracy performance score by 25% on average while
reducing the reasoning tokens by 4%. For the research insight discovery
application, we demonstrate that an insight library learned from ICLR
papers in one year can cover the core technical contributions of over
80% of accepted papers in the next year. FoT enables LLM-based systems
to function not only as performance-driven solvers, but also as tools
for decision support and insight discovery.

## 2 Related Work

Multi-Agent Collaboration. Extensive prior multi-agent works focus on
enabling agents to solve a given complicated task in a collaborative
way. A common paradigm involves decomposing a task into smaller
subtasks, assigning each to an individual agent, and aggregating the
partial results \[[48](#bib.bib35), [30](#bib.bib4), [6](#bib.bib36),
[5](#bib.bib38), [20](#bib.bib40), e.g.,\]. Other existing approaches
include multi-agent debate \[[16](#bib.bib25)\] or allowing multiple
agents to repeatedly perform the same task and vote on a solution
\[[34](#bib.bib37), [43](#bib.bib33), [51](#bib.bib34)\]. Previous works
also study large-scale agentic knowledge exchange by building concrete
workflows for agent laboratories \[[27](#bib.bib19)\], or simulating
research communities \[[40](#bib.bib6), [42](#bib.bib20)\]. Rather than
using multiple agents to handle different components of a single task or
building end-to-end workflows to simulate complicated systems, in FoT,
each client runs a local agent that solves problems independently and
the server aggregates reasoning traces from the problem-solving
processes to distill shared insights
(Figure [1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 Federation over Text ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")).

Collaborative and Federated Learning. Collaborative or federated
learning (FL) \[[21](#bib.bib3)\] aggregates model parameters from
multiple clients while keeping data local. Existing literature on
federated agents primarily focuses on training language models in the
classical parameter or gradient-level aggregation framework
\[[15](#bib.bib9)\], which can be expensive and insufficient for
capturing high-level abstract reasoning strategies. Social learning
\[[22](#bib.bib5)\] allows teacher agents to generate synthetic examples
or abstract prompts that are aggregated to train a student model in a
single-task setting. FL and FoT share interesting connections
(Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Analogies Between Federated/Distributed Learning and FoT ‣ 3 Federation over Text ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"));
FoT operates in the semantic space while being compatible with
heterogeneous agent models and task domains.

LLM Skills and Recursive Self-Improvement. To embed past experience into
LLM-based agents, existing approaches such as Anthropic
Skills \[[3](#bib.bib45)\], Agents.md¹¹ 1
[https://agents.md/](https://agents.md/) , vibe
research \[[47](#bib.bib21)\], and Scientific
Skills \[[10](#bib.bib22)\] focus on providing concrete skills for
executing specific tasks rather than generalizable, abstract insights.
Moreover, they require some extent of human-guided process to generate
skills, whereas FoT generates reusable insights automatically without
any human intervention; even labels indicating whether an answer is
correct are not required. ExpeL \[[49](#bib.bib54)\] stores an agent’s
past successful trajectories along with reflections on successes and
failures, relying on explicit labeling. There is also extensive research
on improving agent reasoning through self-reflection, self-improvement,
or context engineering \[[39](#bib.bib27), [7](#bib.bib2),
[53](#bib.bib8), [41](#bib.bib26), [44](#bib.bib28), [38](#bib.bib31),
[31](#bib.bib29), [54](#bib.bib32), [37](#bib.bib30)\]. However, they do
not consider jointly learning insights by distilling reasoning traces
across independent agents solving different, but related tasks.
Moreover, FoT can adopt any existing self-improvement method as the
local thinking approach
(Section [6.1](#S6.SS1 "6.1 Effects of Local Reasoning Strategies ‣ 6 Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"))
and aggregate their traces to iteratively form generalizable insights.

Another line of work on agent improvement requires gradient optimization
via various forms of fine-tuning or reinforcement
learning \[[52](#bib.bib23), [32](#bib.bib24)\]. FoT operates purely on
the inference level without any fine-tuning or complicated supervision.
In addition, these approaches are mainly designed for solving a single
task and do not consider federation. Hence, in this paper, we only
compare with methods that only involve API access without computing
gradients.

## 3 Federation over Text

In this section, we propose our federation over text framework and
discuss its connections with federated learning (i.e., gradient
aggregation) \[[21](#bib.bib3)\]. Federated learning (FL) focuses on
training a shared global model to serve existing and future clients,
whereas FoT aims to build an insight library that helps both existing
and new agents to better solve a variety of tasks. In the most common FL
workflow, the server broadcasts the current global model to each client,
who then performs local training on their local data and transmits the
local model updates back to the server. The server aggregates the model
updates to form a new global model. This iterative process repeats until
convergence. At a high level, in FoT, at each round, each client runs a
local agent (any base LLM(s)) who solves its local task with the help of
the current insight library, and sends the reasoning traces to the
server. The server merges them to update the library and distributes it
to all agents for the next round. We present the overall workflow of FL
and FoT in
[Figure 1](#S3.F1 "In 3 Federation over Text ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
as well as the pseudocode of both algorithms in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Pseudo Algorithms ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning").

Figure 1: Workflow of federation over (accumulated) gradients and
federation over text. See pseudocode in
Algorithms [1](#algorithm1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix B Pseudo Algorithms ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
and
[2](#algorithm2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ Appendix B Pseudo Algorithms ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
in the appendix.

In the workflow of FoT (the right subfigure of
[Figure 1](#S3.F1 "In 3 Federation over Text ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")),
each of the (potentially many) decentralized agents solves a specific
problem or task, using a selected base LLM. These tasks can span
different domains such as mathematical reasoning, coding, and scientific
question-answering. Given a task (e.g., a collection of math questions),
an agent first solves the task (e.g., generates solutions), then
reflects on whether the reasoning process contains reusable techniques
and what key skills can be extracted. Instead of uploading complete, raw
reasoning histories, each agent generates a logic-level reasoning trace
for each problem based on its solution and reflections, specifying when
and how to apply the extracted skills via step-by-step instructions.
Agents then share these shorter, summarized messages with the server,
while keeping problem instances and raw histories local.

In each round, after collecting traces, the server needs to aggregate
them to update the insight library. We develop one specific aggregation
technique that distills high-level insights rather than simply
concatenating reasoning traces. In particular, the server first clusters
reasoning traces that share similar skills, and then uncovers
connections among traces that solve the same problem using different
skills and can potentially be merged. Finally, the server broadcasts the
updated insights library to all agents for the next iteration. The
aggregated library can be re-used as an external reference to improve
the reasoning of either existing agents or future agents that are not in
the current network. Unlike parameter updates, the resulting knowledge
is human-readable and interpretable. This improves transparency and
enables cross-domain transfer of reasoning strategies. We provide all
the designed prompts that we use in
Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G Complete Prompts ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning").

Local Reasoning and Global Aggregation Strategies. We note that many
self-improvement methods proposed by prior works \[[39](#bib.bib27),
[7](#bib.bib2), [53](#bib.bib8), [41](#bib.bib26), [44](#bib.bib28),
e.g.,\] can be plugged into FoT to generate the reasoning traces sent to
the server. In our experiments
(Section [6.1](#S6.SS1 "6.1 Effects of Local Reasoning Strategies ‣ 6 Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")),
we plug several different local thinking methods into FoT. We also
enable calling external tools
([Section 4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Real-World Daily Tasks ‣ 4 Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")).
Additionally, we note that while we currently use curated prompts to
perform global aggregation in the text space
(Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G Complete Prompts ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")),
the aggregation step of FoT can adopt other techniques developed for
general context compression \[[1](#bib.bib16), [2](#bib.bib17)\]
([Section 6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2 Effects of Global Aggregation Strategies ‣ 6 Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")).
FoT is modular in that local or global procedures can adapt various
algorithms/prompts, and be handled via heterogeneous LLM models
(Section [6](#S6 "6 Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")).

### 3.1 Analogies Between Federated/Distributed Learning and FoT

We reiterate that there are rich connections between FL and FoT. In
particular, in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.1 Analogies Between Federated/Distributed Learning and FoT ‣ 3 Federation over Text ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
we summarize how their algorithmic components can be mapped between each
other. For instance, in FL, clients may adopt different optimization
methods to solve local subproblems. Analogously, in FoT, each agent may
leverage distinct local reasoning strategies and prompt designs to
generate traces.

|                      |                                                                   |                                                                |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Components           | Federation over Gradients                                         | Federation over Text (FoT)                                     |
| Learning Objective   | Learn a global model that generalizes to test data or new clients | Learn an insight library that improves the reasoning of agents |
| Learning Work        | Local training via any optimization method                        | Local task solving via any self-improvement approach           |
| Data Minimization    | Share model updates rather than raw data                          | Share abstracted reasoning traces rather than raw instances    |
| Local $`\to`$ Server | Clients upload model weights or gradients                         | Agents upload reasoning traces from problem-solving            |
| Server Aggregation   | Averaging over model weights or gradients                         | Aggregating over reasoning traces (text) using curated prompts |
| Server $`\to`$ Local | Current learnt global model                                       | Current curated insight library                                |
| Personalization      | Maintaining personalized local models                             | Addressing diverse local tasks across different domains.       |

Table 1: Connections between Federated Learning over Gradients and
Federation over Text (FoT).

Inspired by techniques from distributed or federated learning, FoT
allows for an interesting design space to improve efficiency and
effectiveness of multi-agent collaborative reasoning
(Section [4](#S4 "4 Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")).
It is worth continuing to explore the design space of FoT, such as
personalization strategies and handling other forms of distribution
drifts across agents, which we leave for future work.

## 4 Applications of FoT

In this section, we study four applications demonstrating how FoT
enhances reasoning performance and efficiency, including mathematical
problem-solving with varying levels of difficulty
([Section 4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Mathematical Problem Solving ‣ 4 Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")),
cross-domain collaboration involving math, scientific QA, coding, and
others
([Section 4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Multi-Domain Collaboration ‣ 4 Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")),
real-world daily
tasks ([Section 4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Real-World Daily Tasks ‣ 4 Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")),
and ML research insight discovery
([Section 4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Research Insight Discovery ‣ 4 Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")).
Our code and experiments are open sourced at
[https://github.com/dixiyao/FoT](https://github.com/dixiyao/FoT).

### 4.1 Mathematical Problem Solving

In this application, the agents’ goal is to solve math problems. There
are eight agents, each working on one of eight datasets with varying
levels of difficulty, AIME24 \[[45](#bib.bib12)\],
AIME25 \[[46](#bib.bib13)\], AMC, CCEE, CNMO, WLPMC, V202412 Hard, and
V202505 Hard from LiveMathBench \[[17](#bib.bib14)\]. We experiment with
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Gemini-3.0-Pro as two choices of the
base LLM.

[Figure 2](#S4.F2 "In 4.1 Mathematical Problem Solving ‣ 4 Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
shows the results averaged on eight benchmarks. Numbers on each
benchmark are in
[Section D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 Mathematical Problem Solving ‣ Appendix D Complete Experiments for Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning").
FoT can help reduce loops (i.e., the number of times repeated sentences
are generated during the reasoning process). With the presence of an
insight library, agents generate fewer tokens while achieving better
final performance. Additionally, FoT reduces the number of loops,
indicating less repeated reasoning content. Note that our insight
library size is manageable, which is helpful for communication
efficiency and reducing the context length for LLMs. For DeepSeek, by
Round 3, we generate 249 reasoning traces in total (33K tokens) and
aggregate them into 11 insights (3K tokens). For Gemini 3.0 Pro, we
generate 549 traces (53K tokens) and aggregate them into 37 insights
(12K tokens). The cost of uploading reasoning traces and downloading
insights is moderate, yielding substantial improvements in utilities. We
study the effects of insight library size in
Section [6.4](#S6.SS4 "6.4 Effects of Insight Library Size ‣ 6 Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning").

Figure 2: Comparison of reasoning accuracies and efficiency (measured by
average number of reasoning tokens and total loops), averaged over eight
math benchmarks.

### 4.2 Multi-Domain Collaboration

Figure 3: Accuracies and average number of generated tokens during the
reasoning process across math, scientific QA, and coding benchmarks.
Round 1 represents isolated agents. Insight libraries improve reasoning
across domains while reducing token usage.

Figure 4: Comparisons of the true-thinking score
(TTS) \[[50](#bib.bib18)\], measuring reasoning steps whose removal
would lead the agent to a different answer. FoT exhibits fewer
decorative reasoning steps.

In this section, we go a step further to understand how FoT can retrieve
cross-domain knowledge, helping agents working on different but related
domain tasks collaborate and improve each other’s reasoning. We first
choose AIME24 and AIME25 for math tasks, GPQA and
GPQA-diamond \[[26](#bib.bib11)\] for scientific question-answering (QA)
tasks, and LiveCodeBench (version 6, Hard) \[[8](#bib.bib15)\] for
coding. At first glance, these three domains appear loosely related.
However, apart from the performance improvement demonstrated in
[Figure 3](#S4.F3 "In Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 Multi-Domain Collaboration ‣ 4 Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
FoT generates insights that highlight underlying conceptual similarities
across multiple domains. We let each agent mark which insights
contribute most to the reasoning process. In
[Section D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Multi-Domain Collaboration ‣ Appendix D Complete Experiments for Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
we present two case studies illustrating the content of insights, which
insights are used, and how they are applied during the reasoning process
to arrive at correct solutions. These examples show that insights from
one domain (e.g., math, Sudoku) can be used to correct the reasoning
processes of tasks in a different domain (e.g., chemistry). Second, we
also experiment with cross-domain collaboration on more challenging
benchmarks, including Humanity’s Last Exam \[[24](#bib.bib46)\], and
show that even when most reasoning traces originate from incorrect
answers, the insight library can still improve overall performance
(Table [9](#A4.T9 "Table 9 ‣ D.2 Multi-Domain Collaboration ‣ Appendix D Complete Experiments for Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")).
From
[Figure 3](#S4.F3 "In Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 Multi-Domain Collaboration ‣ 4 Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
we can also observe diminishing gains after round 3, suggesting
convergence of the insight library.

True-Thinking Abilities. To see how FoT can also reduce decorative
reasoning, we report the ‘true-thinking score’ \[[50](#bib.bib18)\] in
the multi-domain collaboration application. The true-thinking score
(TTS) measures the proportion of reasoning steps whose removal would
lead the agent to a different answer, thus serving as a proxy metric of
effective reasoning. From
[Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In 4.2 Multi-Domain Collaboration ‣ 4 Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
we can see that FoT increases the score compared with the baseline,
indicating that insights generated by FoT can help agents skip redundant
reasoning steps.

OpenClaw agents and FoT resolve all tasks in PinchBench. FoT can greatly

[Section D.3.1](#A4.SS3.SSS1 "D.3.1 Cost Evaluation for the Application of OpenClaw ‣ D.3 Real-World Daily Tasks ‣ Appendix D Complete Experiments for Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),

In this application, FoT positions agents as tools for decision support
in daily work tasks. We use OpenClaw \[[23](#bib.bib47)\], experimenting
with both Gemini 3.1 Pro and Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite as backend models. We
evaluate on PinchBench \[[12](#bib.bib48)\], which covers tasks such as
web research and stock analysis. Each OpenClaw agent is assigned to one
task and produces reasoning traces from its execution trajectory. FoT
aggregates these traces into a shared insight library, insight.md, which
agents then use alongside pre-defined tools and skills to complete
tasks. We compare with three additional baselines where we (1) append
all agent trajectories into a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
datastore for each agent, or (2) equip each agent with 52 pre-defined
OpenClaw skills. Agents perform independent reasoning in both cases. (3)
ExpeL \[[49](#bib.bib54)\]. We repeat all experiments five times and
report both average and best-case performance.

We report core results in
[Table 2](#S4.T2 "In 4.3 Real-World Daily Tasks ‣ 4 Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
across high, medium, and low thinking levels. At the high-thinking
level, OpenClaw agents using the insight library achieve an average
accuracy that exceeds even the best isolated-agent accuracy. The insight
library can also lower overall token consumption in the Gemini 3.1 Pro
(High) and Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite experiments. Similar to the
transferability experiments in
[Section 4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Mathematical Problem Solving ‣ 4 Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
FoT enables medium- and low-thinking agents to reach performance
comparable to isolated agents at high and medium thinking levels,
respectively. In the Gemini 2.5 experiments, most of the traces come
from faulty reasoning, yet FoT is not misled and still achieves accuracy
above 50%, demonstrating robustness to noisy traces. Results of
comparing with two additional enhanced isolated reasoning baselines and
ExpeL \[[49](#bib.bib54)\] are in
[Section D.3.2](#A4.SS3.SSS2 "D.3.2 Comparing with Additional Baselines ‣ D.3 Real-World Daily Tasks ‣ Appendix D Complete Experiments for Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
where we again observe the significant superiority of FoT, especially
when solving cross-domain tasks.

Since these tasks involve multi-round interactions and tool use rather
than simple answer generation, we also measure wall-clock execution
time, defined as the time from sending a query to the agent until task
completion, including tool execution. We observe that latency decreases
when the thinking level is increased from low to high, even though
higher thinking levels generate more tokens due to more efficient
calling of suitable tools. More details and two concrete examples to
illustrate how agents with and without the library handle these cases
are in
[Section D.3.3](#A4.SS3.SSS3 "D.3.3 Examples of Tool Usage ‣ D.3 Real-World Daily Tasks ‣ Appendix D Complete Experiments for Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning").

### 4.4 Research Insight Discovery

We demonstrate that with FoT, agents collectively extract and synthesize
insights across diverse areas of machine learning research. This differs
from work on end-to-end agentic workflows that execute the full
scientific pipeline and generate submission-ready
papers \[[19](#bib.bib52), [27](#bib.bib19), [9](#bib.bib42),
[33](#bib.bib43), [35](#bib.bib41), [20](#bib.bib40),
[29](#bib.bib44)\], which is not what we focus on here. In our setting,
each agent is assigned one or more papers to read and identify research
questions. FoT then curates an insight library of actionable and
generalizable research insights. We evaluate how many future papers
could have been guided by these insights as core contributions, using
four criteria: concrete methodological usage, how the method is
presented, whether the paper’s core contribution would fundamentally
change without the insight, and whether the insight is novel; see
[Prompt 6](#prompt6 "In G.1 Prompts for Our Instantiation of FoT ‣ Appendix G Complete Prompts ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
in the appendix. Note that methods requiring explicit labeling cannot
handle such applications, as there is no explicit success signal for
reading papers.

We consider two settings depending on whether the base LLM may have seen
the evaluation papers during pretraining. In Setting 1, 1574 agents each
read one accepted ICLR 2023 paper, and we evaluate on accepted ICLR 2024
papers using Gemini 3.0 Pro²² 2 We use the checkpoint
gemini-3.0-pro-preview released on November 18, 2025. for all agents and
the server. Since this model may already contain knowledge of ICLR 2024
papers, Setting 2 uses Gemini 2.0 Flash³³ 3 We use the checkpoint
gemini-2.0-flash-001 released on April 9, 2025. to read ICLR 2024
papers, and we evaluate on ICLR 2025 papers. Gemini 2.0 Flash has no
access to 2025 papers because its cutoff date is before the ICLR 2025
submission deadline.

We compare against two baselines. First, we query a standalone Gemini
model to generate the top 200 insights using ICLR keywords and the same
insight definition, then evaluate whether these insights guide papers in
the following year. Second, we use retrieval-augmented generation
(RAG) \[[14](#bib.bib7)\] to build a datastore of all selected papers
from the previous year and ask the LLM to generate the top 200 insights
using retrieved content as reference. These baselines test whether FoT
improves insight discovery beyond the LLM’s standalone capability and
simple retrieval over prior papers. By default, we use Gemini 3.0 Pro as
judge and report results in
[Table 3](#S4.T3 "In 4.4 Research Insight Discovery ‣ 4 Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning").
We further cross-validate with Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite,
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in
[Section D.4.1](#A4.SS4.SSS1 "D.4.1 Cross Model Validation for Research Insight Discovery ‣ D.4 Research Insight Discovery ‣ Appendix D Complete Experiments for Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning").
FoT insights achieve the highest guidance rate across evaluations by all
four models. For instance, when evaluated by Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite,
directly prompting Gemini 3.0 Pro guides only 2.2% of ICLR 2024 papers,
whereas FoT insights guide 70.6%. In addition to LLM-based judging, we
manually verify the generated insights and provide a subset in
Appendix [H.1](#A8.SS1 "H.1 Representative Insights ‣ Appendix H Insights, Raw Reasoning Processes, and Reasoning Traces ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning").

|                   |                  |                          |      |           |        |                           |      |           |        |                                |      |           |        |
| ----------------- | ---------------- | ------------------------ | ---- | --------- | ------ | ------------------------- | ---- | --------- | ------ | ------------------------------ | ---- | --------- | ------ |
| Setting           | Model            | Isolated Agents (Gemini) |      |           |        | RAG (Gemini + All Papers) |      |           |        | FoT (Gemini + Insight Library) |      |           |        |
|                   |                  | Overall                  | Oral | Spotlight | Poster | Overall                   | Oral | Spotlight | Poster | Overall                        | Oral | Spotlight | Poster |
| 1 (23 $`\to`$ 24) | Gemini 3.0 Pro   | 41.3                     | 70.9 | 73.8      | 33.3   | 66.5                      | 58.1 | 69.2      | 66.4   | 67.4                           | 67.4 | 68.7      | 67.2   |
| 2 (24 $`\to`$ 25) | Gemini 2.0 Flash | 0.7                      | 0.5  | 0.8       | 0.7    | 77.4                      | 63.4 | 67.4      | 79.6   | 82.4                           | 82.2 | 82.1      | 82.4   |

Table 3: Percentage of papers guided by insights generated from
different models. FoT improves overall guidance rate over the baseline
of independently solving tasks without the library (‘Isolated Agents’)
and the baseline that simply stores previous tasks in RAG for retrieval
(‘RAG’).

A potential concern with centralized agentic systems, such as
server-deployed auto-research agents, is that they may require access to
full research papers. For unpublished or unlicensed papers, such sharing
can raise intellectual property concerns. In contrast, FoT uploads only
abstract metacognitive summaries, as illustrated in
[Section H.3](#A8.SS3 "H.3 Example Reasoning Traces in ‣ Appendix H Insights, Raw Reasoning Processes, and Reasoning Traces ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
without exposing paper details or sensitive experimental data
([Section 5](#S5 "5 Properties of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")).
This design allows users to leverage local agentic assistants while
still benefiting from global insights produced by the server. The shared
insight library further supports iterative improvement, helping both
agents and humans refine ideas and develop future research.

## 5 Properties of FoT

Transferability Across New Models and Tasks. We investigate whether (1)
the insight library curated by one LLM model is compatible with a
different model for reasoning, and (2) whether the library curated in
one application can be transferred to new, unseen tasks.
[Table 4](#S5.T4 "In 5 Properties of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
demonstrates that FoT allows for the decoupling of the base LLMs for
actual reasoning and the models for building the shared insight library.
Moreover, we observe that an insight library generated by a weaker model
(DeepSeek) can supervise and improve the performance of stronger ones
(Gemini 3.0 Pro) (last two rows of
[Table 4](#S5.T4 "In 5 Properties of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")).
This indicates that a variant of ‘weak-to-strong generalization’ can
happen in the text space, beyond the gradient space studied in prior
works \[[4](#bib.bib10), e.g.,\].

|                         |                       |       |                  |          |
| ----------------------- | --------------------- | ----- | ---------------- | -------- |
| Reasoning Model         | Insight Library Model | Avg   | \# Output Tokens | \# Loops |
| Isolated DeepSeek       | N/A                   | 0.537 | 6312             | 7        |
| DeepSeek                | Gemini 3.0 Pro        | 0.625 | 4317             | 4        |
| Isolated Gemini 3.0 Pro | N/A                   | 0.846 | 891              | 3        |
| Gemini 3.0 Pro          | DeepSeek              | 0.902 | 745              | 0        |

Table 4: Evaluation of decoupling insight library models and reasoning
models on math problem-solving. Insights produced by stronger models
(Gemini 3.0 Pro) consistently benefit weaker agents (DeepSeek), while
libraries from weaker agents can also improve stronger ones.

We further investigate how the insight library generalizes to unseen
tasks that are not involved in the library construction process. For
mathematical problems and multi-domain collaboration benchmarks, we
split the tasks into two disjoint halves: one half is used for insight
library construction, while the other half is reserved exclusively for
evaluating the library. For real-world daily tasks, we use the old 23
tasks from the evolving PinchBench V1 for insight library construction,
and evaluate generalization on the newly introduced 124 tasks spanning
53 categories in PinchBench V2. Same as the previous settings, we
conduct mathematical problem solving and multi-domain collaboration
experiments using 3 different random seeds, and evaluate real-world
daily tasks using 5 different random seeds.

|                   |                 |                              |                       |                            |                        |                       |
| ----------------- | --------------- | ---------------------------- | --------------------- | -------------------------- | ---------------------- | --------------------- |
|                   |                 | Mathematical Problem Solving |                       | Multi-Domain Collaboration | Real-World Daily Tasks |                       |
|                   | Algorithm       | Gemini 3.1 Pro               | Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite | Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite      | Gemini 3.1 Pro         | Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite |
| Existing Problems | Isolated Agents | 88.50$`\pm`$1.80             | 88.24$`\pm`$3.51      | 82.36$`\pm`$1.88           | 76.29$`\pm`$3.39       | 20.12$`\pm`$6.21      |
|                   | FoT             | 90.10$`\pm`$0.89             | 90.12$`\pm`$2.00      | 85.00$`\pm`$0.60           | 84.82$`\pm`$2.33       | 52.11$`\pm`$1.26      |
| New Problems      | Isolated Agents | 89.13$`\pm`$2.19             | 87.33$`\pm`$1.64      | 84.96$`\pm`$1.53           | 85.03$`\pm`$1.51       | 34.60$`\pm`$1.42      |
|                   | FoT             | 89.66$`\pm`$1.22             | 89.94$`\pm`$0.81      | 86.60$`\pm`$0.29           | 86.67$`\pm`$1.05       | 36.67$`\pm`$0.82      |

Table 5: Average accuracies across different tasks and experimental
settings on existing and new, unseen tasks. For FoT, agents utilize the
shared insight library for both sets of problems, whereas the isolated
reasoning agents perform inference independently without access to any
shared library.

We observe that FoT achieves the largest performance gains during
test-time learning, while still maintaining consistent improvements on
unseen tasks. This demonstrates that the insight library can
continuously benefit newly introduced agents, enabling knowledge
transfer and generalization beyond the tasks used during library
construction. Complete results on each benchmark are in
[Section E.1](#A5.SS1 "E.1 Transferability ‣ Appendix E Complete Experiments for Properties of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning").
In
[Section E.1](#A5.SS1 "E.1 Transferability ‣ Appendix E Complete Experiments for Properties of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
we also verify that new agents on unseen tasks in
Claw-Eval \[[36](#bib.bib49)\] ($`199`$ agents) can benefit from an
insight library generated on PinchBench ($`23`$ agents). The library
transfers effectively across agents and tasks, improving performance
while reducing token usage.

Safeguarding Raw Problem Instances. In addition to improving reasoning
effectiveness and efficiency, FoT brings about the side benefit of
safeguarding raw problem instances. First, we observe that the uploaded
abstracted reasoning traces do not contain original problem or task
descriptions. We employ a strong multi-turn prompt-stealing
attacker \[[28](#bib.bib50)\] to reconstruct the agent input from given
reasoning traces. The token-level F1 scores between the reconstructed
and original inputs are smaller than 0.25. Also, no personal
identifiable information (PII) is leaked. Second, we verify that the
insight library does not contain answers to the questions, preventing
agents from directly retrieving answers via shortcuts. Using shingle
intersection and a strict 4-gram matching, we compute Jaccard similarity
between the insight library and ground-truth answers, as well as between
reasoning traces and input questions. We observe near-zero similarity.
Full details and quantitative results are provided in
[Section E.2](#A5.SS2 "E.2 Safeguarding Raw Problem Instances ‣ Appendix E Complete Experiments for Properties of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning").

## 6 Ablation Studies

In this section, we empirically study the effects of key FoT parameters.
[Sections 6.1](#S6.SS1 "6.1 Effects of Local Reasoning Strategies ‣ 6 Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
[6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2 Effects of Global Aggregation Strategies ‣ 6 Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
and [6.3](#S6.SS3 "6.3 Effects of Heterogeneous Local and Server Agent Models ‣ 6 Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
examine the impacts of varying local reasoning strategies, server
aggregation strategies, and heterogeneous base LLM models, respectively.
We further study FoT performance under different library sizes
([Section 6.4](#S6.SS4 "6.4 Effects of Insight Library Size ‣ 6 Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"))
and different agent participation scenarios
([Section 6.5](#S6.SS5 "6.5 Effects of Agent Participation ‣ 6 Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")).

### 6.1 Effects of Local Reasoning Strategies

In this section, we conduct ablations to (1) examine how our reasoning
trace extraction differs from existing mechanisms, and (2) verify that
FoT is flexible and supports a variety of local reasoning and
self-improvement approaches. We compare with the original prompts
([Section G.3](#A7.SS3 "G.3 Prompts for Metacognitive Reuse [] ‣ Appendix G Complete Prompts ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"))
in work of [Didolkar et al. \[7\]](#bib.bib2), which we adapt from, and
other agent reasoning and self-improvement approaches such as Agentic
Context Engineering (ACE) \[[44](#bib.bib28)\],
HyperAgents \[[41](#bib.bib26)\], and Evolving
Prompt \[[31](#bib.bib29)\]. A subset of core results are reported in
Table [6](#S6.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 6.1 Effects of Local Reasoning Strategies ‣ 6 Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
and detailed implementation and full results on more applications are
provided in
[Section F.1](#A6.SS1 "F.1 Effects of Local Reasoning Strategies ‣ Appendix F Complete Experiments for Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning").

Table 6: Average accuracies of using different local reasoning
strategies in each algorithm in math problem solving tasks
(LiveMathBench).

We see that FoT with different local reasoning methods can improve over
their ‘Isolated Agents’ baseline where each agent solves tasks using the
corresponding reasoning method separately. Using our designed prompts
improves over variants with other local reasoning methods in most cases,
yielding an average +8.1% accuracy gain, along with fewer generated
tokens and reasoning loops
([Section F.1](#A6.SS1 "F.1 Effects of Local Reasoning Strategies ‣ Appendix F Complete Experiments for Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")).
FoT with HyperAgents as the local reasoning method serves as a strong
alternative in some cases. A potential concern with HyperAgents is that
uploading evolved prompts may introduce privacy risks, as these prompts
can contain descriptions of the underlying questions.

### 6.2 Effects of Global Aggregation Strategies

We demonstrate that FoT is flexible to support different global
aggregation algorithms on the server side. In particular, we evaluate
the baseline of simply appending the shared traces, and other context
compression techniques, including Chain-of-Density
(CoD) \[[1](#bib.bib16)\] and Context Compaction from Claude
Cookbook \[[2](#bib.bib17)\] (denoted as ‘Compaction’). For all three
baselines, we vary the corresponding compression ratio parameters to
illustrate the tradeoffs between task performance (accuracies or
research idea guidance rate) and efficiency (number of reasoning tokens
as well as library sizes).

Figure 5: Accuracy and number of output tokens using different
server-side algorithms on LiveMathBench. FoT achieves the highest
accuracy with a moderate number of tokens, providing a good trade-off
between accuracy and efficiency.

Figure 6: Percentage of papers guided by insights using different
server-side aggregation. FoT generates a reasonably-sized library
guiding most papers. General context compression methods might not be
the most suitable for the task.

We see that on math problem-solving, simply concatenating all traces
results in the worst accuracy. Even when the total tokens remain within
the context window, long prompts can still lead to ‘context loss’,
observed by previous works \[[18](#bib.bib39), e.g.,\]. Varying the
percentage of traces to append (75% and 50% randomly picked) does not
help much. CoD and Compaction (plugged into FoT) can be effective and
yield performance gains over the independent reasoning baselines,
although the accuracy improvement is smaller than that achieved by our
proposed prompts. In the ML insight discovery task
([Figure 6](#S6.F6 "In 6.2 Effects of Global Aggregation Strategies ‣ 6 Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")),
we observe that CoD adopts an aggressive context compression strategy
and thus produces far fewer tokens. However, the generated insights are
not sufficiently satisfactory. For Compaction, the guidance rate
increases as the library size increases, but achieving a good guidance
rate requires a large number of tokens. FoT with our designed
aggregation captures shared patterns without over-generalizing and
produces more meaningful insights at a modest size.

### 6.3 Effects of Heterogeneous Local and Server Agent Models

We further demonstrate the flexibility of FoT in how it is compatible
with different agent models deployed on the local clients or the server.
Full results are provided in
[Section F.2](#A6.SS2 "F.2 Effects of Heterogeneous Local and Server Agent Models ‣ Appendix F Complete Experiments for Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning").
On math problem solving, with Gemini 3.0 Pro as local agents and
DeepSeek as the server model, FoT reaches 88.1%, compared with 84.6% for
isolated reasoning and 92.8% when both server and agents use Gemini 3.0
Pro. With DeepSeek as local agents and Gemini 3.0 Pro as the server, FoT
reaches a 58.0% accuracy, compared with 53.7% in isolation and 55.3%
when both sides use DeepSeek. These results suggest that FoT remains
effective across heterogeneous LLM configurations, with larger gains
when the server model is stronger. Similar conclusions hold for research
insight discovery.
[Table 25](#A6.T25 "In F.2 Effects of Heterogeneous Local and Server Agent Models ‣ Appendix F Complete Experiments for Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
in
[Section F.2](#A6.SS2 "F.2 Effects of Heterogeneous Local and Server Agent Models ‣ Appendix F Complete Experiments for Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
further demonstrates that when we have local agents each using different
LLMs but working on the same task, FoT still provides performance gains.
While deploying all modules with the strongest LLM yields the best
performance, users can select lighter alternatives and leverage FoT’s
flexibility in specific scenarios.

### 6.4 Effects of Insight Library Size

In
[Figure 7](#S6.F7 "In 6.4 Effects of Insight Library Size ‣ 6 Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
we vary the insight library size and observe that, without strict
constraints on the total number of insights, FoT naturally reaches a
favorable tradeoff between library size and performance at 20 insights,
as performance improves only marginally when increasing the library size
from 20 to 200. Details are provided in
[Section F.3](#A6.SS3 "F.3 Effects of Insight Library Size ‣ Appendix F Complete Experiments for Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning").

### 6.5 Effects of Agent Participation

We further analyze the impact of varying the number of participating
agents in FoT. For research insight discovery, performance improves as
the total number of papers read increases. When the total number of
papers is fixed, the number of agents has only a minor impact, with more
agents yielding slight additional gains. Since these results align with
intuition, we defer the details to
[Section F.4](#A6.SS4 "F.4 Effects of Agent Participation ‣ Appendix F Complete Experiments for Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning").

We further examine how individual agents contribute to the insight
library through two settings: ‘Include One’, where only one fixed local
agent continuously contributes reasoning traces while all agents use the
resulting library for inference, and ‘Exclude One’, where the library is
constructed from all agents except one. As shown in
[Section 6.4](#S6.SS4 "6.4 Effects of Insight Library Size ‣ 6 Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
every agent improves performance when acting as the sole contributor,
but none matches the performance achieved when all agents contribute,
indicating that FoT benefits from broad agent participation.
[Section 6.4](#S6.SS4 "6.4 Effects of Insight Library Size ‣ 6 Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
also shows that V202505 Hard is the most influential agent, as it yields
the largest improvement over isolated agents when included alone and
causes the largest performance drop when excluded. We provide detailed
performance of each agent in
[Section F.4](#A6.SS4 "F.4 Effects of Agent Participation ‣ Appendix F Complete Experiments for Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning").
In both settings, agents are evaluated on data that are partially unseen
during library construction, yet the insight library still improves
performance.

## 7 Conclusion, Limitations, and Future Work

In this work, we have proposed the first federated-like multi-agent
reasoning framework, Federation over Text (FoT), which enables multiple
agents (each solving a task) to collaboratively learn an insight library
by sharing and aggregating local reasoning traces iteratively. On the
other hand, semantic-level optimization may be a double-edged sword due
to inherent LLM hallucinations, which might introduce erroneous
reasoning traces into the insight library. Mitigating this fundamental
challenge is beyond our current scope, but future work can investigate
hallucination propagation within FoT. We have demonstrated the
effectiveness of FoT across diverse applications, including mathematical
reasoning, cross-domain collaboration, research insight discovery, and
daily OpenClaw agent tasks. Further analyses of reasoning traces,
extracted insights, and ablation studies reveal how insights guide
performance gains and highlight the flexibility of FoT with different
local reasoning strategies and server-side aggregation methods. In
future work, we aim to automate harness design \[[13](#bib.bib51)\] for
FoT. In terms of broader impact, clients may leverage the framework of
FoT for good or harmful use cases, such as injecting adversarial
reasoning traces into the insights.

## Contents

## Appendix A Usage of AI in Writing

We employ large language models (LLMs) primarily to improve the grammar
and clarity of our writing and to assist with coding. Prompts
([Appendix G](#A7 "Appendix G Complete Prompts ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"))
used in this work are partially generated by AI with human step-by-step
guidance. Due to the nature of this research, insight libraries
([Section H.1](#A8.SS1 "H.1 Representative Insights ‣ Appendix H Insights, Raw Reasoning Processes, and Reasoning Traces ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"))
and reasoning traces
([Sections H.2](#A8.SS2 "H.2 Complete Raw Reasoning Process for Case Studies in ‣ Appendix H Insights, Raw Reasoning Processes, and Reasoning Traces ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
and [H.3](#A8.SS3 "H.3 Example Reasoning Traces in ‣ Appendix H Insights, Raw Reasoning Processes, and Reasoning Traces ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"))
are AI generated. All research ideas, directions, and decisions,
however, are independently conceived and carried out by the authors.

## Appendix C Hyperparameters

In
[Section 4](#S4 "4 Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
we provide detailed descriptions of the tasks, datasets, and federation
settings. Here, we additionally report the remaining hyperparameters
used in FoT that were not previously introduced. All experimental
results are reported with pass@1. In
[Sections 4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Mathematical Problem Solving ‣ 4 Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
and [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Multi-Domain Collaboration ‣ 4 Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
experiments are repeated 3 times. In
[Section 4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Real-World Daily Tasks ‣ 4 Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
experiments are repeated 5 times. In
[Section 4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Research Insight Discovery ‣ 4 Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
experiments are run once. We set the temperature to 0.7 and top-$`p`$ to
0.9. We set a repetition penalty of 1.1 for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen7B
and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. For all Gemini models, we use the default
frequency and presence penalty settings.

For local agents, the maximum output token limits are all set to 32,768
for answer generation, 16,384 for reflection, and 8,192 for reasoning
traces. On the server side, the maximum output token limits are set to
32,768 for relationship generation and 16,384 for insight library
construction.

All experiments are conducted in FP16 precision using NVIDIA A100 (40GB)
GPUs when needed.

### D.2 Multi-Domain Collaboration

In the first example, we show that the insight named Constraint
Satisfaction Propagation, originally derived from AIME25 (a mathematics
benchmark), is retrieved and applied to a chemistry problem in the GPQA
Diamond dataset. The key mathematical idea is to model the problem as a
constraint satisfaction problem: the goal is to determine whether the H
atom occupies an axial or equatorial position (i.e., to find a unique
valid state, as described in the insight). The agent then tests
different isomeric forms and verifies them against thermodynamic
constraints.

With the constraints, the agent no longer hallucinates the position of
OH (in Round 2 of FoT), but correctly identifies the Karplus
relationship (in Round 3). The problem instance, our summary of
reasoning traces in two rounds, and the insight text that we extract
from the library are presented below. We present the complete raw
reasoning processes for each round in
Appendix [H.2](#A8.SS2 "H.2 Complete Raw Reasoning Process for Case Studies in ‣ Appendix H Insights, Raw Reasoning Processes, and Reasoning Traces ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning").

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In the second example, we look into a math problem from AIME. The
problem statement, summary of reasoning processes, and
potentially-related insights are shown below. In Round 1, with an empty
insight library (i.e., isolated reasoning), the agent writes out the
formulation but immediately attempts to solve the problem using the
greatest common divisor (GCD), leading to an incorrect computation due
to the complexity of the expression. Inspired by dynamic programming,
specifically the idea of decomposing a problem into smaller overlapping
subproblems, in Round 2, the correct reasoning trace instead breaks the
problem down by expressing $`z_{k}`$ in terms of $`z_{k-1}`$. By
applying a recursive formulation, the solution first derives the general
term and then substitutes the numerical values, ultimately obtaining the
correct answer.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

When examining incorrect reasoning processes (e.g., [Raw Reasoning
Processes 1](#reasoningprocess1 "In H.2 Complete Raw Reasoning Process for Case Studies in ‣ Appendix H Insights, Raw Reasoning Processes, and Reasoning Traces ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
and [3](#reasoningprocess3 "Raw Reasoning Process 3 ‣ H.2 Complete Raw Reasoning Process for Case Studies in ‣ Appendix H Insights, Raw Reasoning Processes, and Reasoning Traces ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
in the Appendix), an interesting phenomenon occurs: there are steps that
are totally irrelevant to the final answer. For example, [Raw Reasoning
Process 3](#reasoningprocess3 "In H.2 Complete Raw Reasoning Process for Case Studies in ‣ Appendix H Insights, Raw Reasoning Processes, and Reasoning Traces ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
first gives a complicated formulation of $`x_{k+1}`$ that does not
contribute to the calculation of $`S_{k+1}`$, since the formulation of
$`S_{k+1}`$ does not come from the first step. As a result, the first
step can be viewed as a ‘decorative thinking’ step. Instead, with FoT’s
insight library, agents do not have to exhibit such decorative thinking
in [Raw Reasoning
Process 4](#reasoningprocess4 "In H.2 Complete Raw Reasoning Process for Case Studies in ‣ Appendix H Insights, Raw Reasoning Processes, and Reasoning Traces ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning").
This indicates that insights as a strong and effective prior can help
LLM agents quickly start from knowledge of previous problems, reducing
the chance of falling into unnecessary or illogical steps. The
experiment of measuring true-thinking score  \[[50](#bib.bib18)\]
further verifies this argument.

For multi-domain collaboration, we supplement our experiments by
incorporating multimodal inputs (including images) on challenging tasks
where agents cannot solve most questions (i.e., isolated agent accuracy
is below 50%). We use the Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE)
benchmark \[[24](#bib.bib46)\]. We deploy three agents (Gemini-3.0-Pro)
to work on HLE, GPQA-Diamond, and V202505-Hard, respectively. Isolated
agent accuracy is below 50% for HLE.
[Table 9](#A4.T9 "In D.2 Multi-Domain Collaboration ‣ Appendix D Complete Experiments for Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
presents the performance gains achieved by FoT on these difficult tasks
across different domains. HLE contains 2,500 questions, GPQA-Diamond
contains 198 questions, and LiveMathBench Hard 2025 contains 100
questions.

As a result, we observe that when the server aggregates traces, most
traces originate from incorrect answers. However, these erroneous
experiences do not degrade the quality of the insight library; FoT can
still aggregate useful information and improve overall performance.

### D.3 Real-World Daily Tasks

#### D.3.1 Cost Evaluation for the Application of OpenClaw

As agents using API services usually incur monetary costs, cost is a
critical concern. In this section, we study whether the additional
steps, including reflection and reasoning trace generation for local
agents, as well as server-side aggregation of the insight library,
introduce significant extra cost. We use the Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview
pricing rules.⁴⁴ 4
[https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing)
For isolated agents, the cost depends on the number of input and output
tokens. For FoT, we calculate the token usage for reflection and
reasoning trace generation, the server-side aggregation, and the input
and output tokens when agents use the generated insight library to solve
tasks. We also compute the cost for the setting where agents only use
the generated library during inference.

The cost is summarized in
[Table 10](#A4.T10 "In D.3.1 Cost Evaluation for the Application of OpenClaw ‣ D.3 Real-World Daily Tasks ‣ Appendix D Complete Experiments for Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning").
We observe that although FoT requires more input tokens compared with
solving tasks separately (since the prompt includes the insight
library), the overall cost is reduced when considering FoT (inference)
as fewer output tokens are generated given the generated library. The
additional cost introduced by FoT is also not substantial, increasing
the total cost only marginally. We believe users would be willing to pay
a small additional cost (e.g., less than half a dollar) to achieve
higher task accuracies.

|                |                 |                |                 |
| -------------- | --------------- | -------------- | --------------- |
| Thinking Level | Isolated Agents | FoT (all)      | FoT (inference) |
| High           | \[0.62, 0.71\]  | \[1.09, 1.14\] | \[0.60, 0.64\]  |
| Medium         | \[0.46, 0.63\]  | \[0.86, 1.12\] | \[0.52, 0.61\]  |
| Low            | \[0.55, 0.62\]  | \[0.95, 1.12\] | \[0.55, 0.62\]  |

Table 10: Cost (USD) for using Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview under different
thinking levels and algorithms. Each cell reports the \[min, max\] range
of cost observed over 5 runs of the experiment for all 25 tasks in
PinchBench. FoT (all) calculates all token usage from reflection,
reasoning trace generation, and server aggregation to inference with the
insight library. FoT (inference) only contains the cost of inference
with access to the insight library.

#### D.3.2 Comparing with Additional Baselines

In addition to isolated agents, we consider two baselines for each local
agent. (1) Each OpenClaw agent is equipped with a set of well-defined
skills. (2) We collect all raw reasoning histories into a RAG datastore,
which is then used by each agent to retrieve past traces when solving
tasks. These two strong baselines are designed to highlight the
performance advantage of FoT. They also reflect contrasting design
philosophies: (1) embedding predefined skills introduces human-curated
external knowledge, whereas FoT emphasizes autonomous generation of
reusable insights; (2) directly sharing raw reasoning histories
conflicts with our objective of not sharing raw questions. For skills,
we install all the 52 skills provided by official OpenClaw ⁵⁵ 5
[https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw).
Among these skills, skills nano-pdf, summarize, github, notion, slack,
weather, and coding agent are highly relevant to PinchBench. From
[Table 11](#A4.T11 "In D.3.2 Comparing with Additional Baselines ‣ D.3 Real-World Daily Tasks ‣ Appendix D Complete Experiments for Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
both skill-augmented agents and those using a RAG datastore improve
performance for the Gemini 2.5 model and can also enhance efficiency.
However, analysis of the execution logs shows that these baselines rely
more heavily on extended reasoning rather than effective tool usage
compared to FoT, resulting in higher generation token counts by Gemini
2.5 Flash Lite. In contrast, FoT more reliably invokes the appropriate
tools, leading to improved performance.

predefined, well-specified skills, and (2) isolated agents augmented
with a RAG datastore constructed from the reasoning histories of all
agents.

We also compare FoT with ExpeL. ExpeL similarly lets an agent run some
tasks and saves past experiences. However, ExpeL is initially designed
for a single agent system and relies on labelling. ExpeL first needs
several training tasks and saves the successful trajectories. For failed
tasks, the agent will reflect on them with more attempts. Apart from raw
successful trajectories, ExpeL also lets the agent reflect on successes
and failures to generate several rules. We convert ExpeL into a
distributed multi-agent version where we choose OpenClaw agents working
on tasks 1-12 on PinchBench as training agents and the rest as
evaluation agents. We tune the hyperparameters and set the max
reflection depth as 3. The maximum number of rules is 20 since FoT
generates 20 insights. The top-K to retrieve from the RAG datastore is 3. For a fair comparison, we first generate an insight library with
agents working on tasks 1-12 in FoT and let the remaining agents use the
insight library to resolve the tasks.

From the results in
[Table 12](#A4.T12 "In D.3.2 Comparing with Additional Baselines ‣ D.3 Real-World Daily Tasks ‣ Appendix D Complete Experiments for Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
we find several pieces of evidence showing that ExpeL is not suitable
for this application. First, ExpeL is initially focused on single-agent
systems and collects experience from the same type of tasks. In
PinchBench, tasks are heterogeneous and often unrelated. For example,
task 13 involves file searching, task 14 involves generating AI images,
and task 15 involves humanizing AI-generated blogs. In contrast, FoT is
designed to learn cross-domain knowledge and can achieve performance
improvements across different task types. Second, ExpeL relies on
labeling and training. This training process incurs substantially higher
costs, more than double the total cost of FoT. Third, as discussed
earlier, directly extending ExpeL into a distributed version requires
uploading raw trajectories.

the run with the minimum execution latency. In Gemini 3.1 Pro, higher
thinking levels tend to reduce execution-time tool calls, and FoT
further decreases tool usage under the medium and high thinking
settings.

#### D.3.3 Examples of Tool Usage

As shown in
[Figure 8](#A4.F8 "In D.3.2 Comparing with Additional Baselines ‣ D.3 Real-World Daily Tasks ‣ Appendix D Complete Experiments for Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
for Gemini 3.1 Pro, the number of execution-tool calls decreases as the
thinking level increases, suggesting that the model can more effectively
identify the most critical tools and solve the task with fewer redundant
calls. This also explains why FoT improves both accuracy and latency
under the medium and high thinking settings: agents can avoid repeated
or unnecessary tool execution by leveraging the shared library.

The first example is the ‘Search and Replace in Files’ task, with task
ID task_skill_search, from PinchBench. We use Gemini 3.1 Pro with the
medium thinking level. To more clearly demonstrate the workflow, we show
each tool-calling step together with its arguments and outputs, while
omitting the model’s reasoning outputs. With the hint from the insight
library, agents directly use functions of READ and EDIT to search and
write the related information rather than using EXEC function with
system functions of ‘cat’. In this way, the agent can organize the
editing in a more structured way and resolve the task more efficiently.

### D.4 Research Insight Discovery

#### D.4.1 Cross Model Validation for Research Insight Discovery

To validate the reliability of the LLM-as-a-judge framework for research
insight discovery, we perform cross-model evaluation using three
additional models beyond Gemini 3.0 Pro. As shown in
[Table 13](#A4.T13 "In D.4.1 Cross Model Validation for Research Insight Discovery ‣ D.4 Research Insight Discovery ‣ Appendix D Complete Experiments for Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
Gemini 3.0 Pro exhibits self-evaluation bias, with the guidance rate for
isolated agents on oral papers dropping from 70.9% to 5.8% when
evaluated by Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite. In contrast, FoT maintains strong
guidance rates under cross-model evaluation by Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite,
indicating better generalization and reduced bias.

## Appendix E Complete Experiments for Properties of FoT

### E.1 Transferability

In addition to transferring the insight library across agents using
different LLMs, we evaluate insight transfer across tasks. Extending the
setup in
[Section 4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Real-World Daily Tasks ‣ 4 Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
we introduce new agents operating on Claw-Eval \[[36](#bib.bib49)\].
Claw-Eval contains 199 daily tasks, including tasks of visual input and
artifact generation, simulated user interaction, trajectory-level
grading, embedded constraint checking, and controlled error injection
which PinchBench does not include. The Claw-Eval metrics also measure
other dimensions such as robustness and safety besides completion. Upon
joining the federation, these agents are initialized with an insight.md
generated from agents previously working on PinchBench. Results in
[Table 14](#A5.T14 "In E.1 Transferability ‣ Appendix E Complete Experiments for Properties of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
show that new agents need fewer inference tokens and hence save cost
with the help of the previous library. We provide detailed results of
the transferability experiments on each math benchmark in
[Table 15](#A5.T15 "In E.1 Transferability ‣ Appendix E Complete Experiments for Properties of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning").

### E.2 Safeguarding Raw Problem Instances

First, we investigate whether the original task description can be
inferred from uploaded reasoning traces. We adopt a strong
prompt-stealing attack setting \[[28](#bib.bib50)\], where the attacker
or an honest-but-curious server aims to reconstruct the original task
prompt from observed traces. In PinchBench daily tasks, the attacker is
given a reasoning trace and must infer the agent’s input, including the
user query and auxiliary information (e.g., documents to be summarized).
The attack consists of two components: a parameter extractor, which
classifies the prompt type into direct user request, role-based (persona
or instructional framing), or in-context (demonstrations or substantial
context), and a prompt extractor, which reconstructs the prompt. The two
components interact for three rounds to refine the output. We use
Gemini-2.5-Pro as the attacking model and evaluate attacks on libraries
generated by FoT using Gemini-3.1-Pro (high thinking) and
Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite.

We use several metrics to measure whether the attacker reconstructs the
original input. We first evaluate reconstruction quality using
character-level similarity, defined as $`\frac{2M}{T}`$, where $`M`$ is
the number of matching characters (in contiguous substrings appearing in
both strings in the same order) and $`T`$ is the total number of
characters across both strings. We also report token-level F1 score and
the extent of personally identifiable information (PII) leakage. Due to
the small size of PinchBench (25 tasks), PII is manually annotated. In
addition, we report the classification accuracy of the parameter
extractor component in the model. The parameter extractor performs worse
than random guessing, indicating that it fails to reliably identify the
prompt structure. In
Table [18](#A5.T18 "Table 18 ‣ E.2 Safeguarding Raw Problem Instances ‣ Appendix E Complete Experiments for Properties of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
we see that both character-level similarity and token-level F1 scores
are low, further confirming that the reconstructed prompts do not
closely match the originals. Prior work \[[28](#bib.bib50)\] suggests
that successful prompt reconstruction typically requires similarity
exceeding 60%, which is not observed in our setting.

At the same time, these metrics are not expected to be zero. Reasoning
traces necessarily retain some task-relevant information to enable
knowledge transfer across agents. If similarities were zero, it would
imply that the traces are entirely unrelated to the original tasks,
i.e., effectively hallucinated and non-informative. Hence, we can draw
the conclusion that reasoning traces are effective at hiding raw problem
instances from the server. More importantly, no personal identity
information can be inferred.

|                       |                 |          |            |                         |
| --------------------- | --------------- | -------- | ---------- | ----------------------- |
| FoT Model             | Char Similarity | Token F1 | PII leaked | Parameter Extractor Acc |
| Gemini 3.1 Pro        | 14.89%          | 22.85%   | 0          | 26.09%                  |
| Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite | 11.94%          | 24.44%   | 0          | 21.74%                  |

Table 18: Prompt stealing attack results. The attacker uses
Gemini-2.5-Pro with PinchBench reasoning traces in FoT to reconstruct
the original input. The low character-level similarity, low token-level
F1, and low parameter-extraction accuracy indicate that the attack fails
to recover the original input, suggesting an effective defense. No
personal identity information (PII) is leaked. The closest
reconstruction achieved by the attacker is inferring that the
instruction involves common file names such as _“ai blog.txt”_ and
_“humanized blog.txt”_.

Second, we adopt a strict $`n`$-gram matching test to check: (1) that
uploaded reasoning traces do not overlap with the original inputs (e.g.,
benchmark questions and ground-truth answers), and (2) that the insight
library does not contain original inputs.

For each application, we append all problem instances together into a
document, and partition the document into 4-gram token shingles.
Problems refer to questions, tasks, or papers depending on the
application. We do the same for answers, insight libraries, and
reasoning traces, separately. Each document is a set of all 4-gram token
shingles. We then evaluate similarities between (a) reasoning traces and
problems, and between (b) the insight library and problems + answers, by
reporting the Jaccard similarities between the two sets of 4-gram tokens
in the corresponding two documents. Prior work on shingle-based
plagiarism detection shows that the choice of $`n`$ in $`n`$-gram
significantly affects similarity estimates, with smaller $`n`$ leading
to inflated overlap due to common phrases and larger $`n`$ being overly
sensitive to minor edits \[[25](#bib.bib53)\]. We adopt 4-gram shingles
as a balanced choice that reduces false positives while remaining
sensitive to meaningful phrase-level reuse.

In
[Table 19](#A5.T19 "In E.2 Safeguarding Raw Problem Instances ‣ Appendix E Complete Experiments for Properties of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
we observe that Jaccard similarity is near zero, indicating that the
reasoning traces have little overlap with raw user questions and
answers, achieving one of the goals of FoT. The zero similarity between
the insight library and the problems further suggests that an adversary
cannot obtain raw problem instances by examining the library.

Table 19: The measurement of overlap between the insight library (IL),
reasoning traces (RT), and problems. \# Problems refer to questions,
tasks, or papers depending on the application. Jaccard similarity is
computed between 4-gram token sets constructed from problem statements,
answers, reasoning traces, and insight libraries.

Furthermore, our work does not focus on studying prompt leakage or
defenses for multi-agent reasoning. Instead, in addition to improving
reasoning effectiveness and efficiency, FoT brings about the side
benefit of data minimization by exposing the underlying logic-level
summarization of the reasoning processes as opposed to raw reasoning
data or task data. A more thorough investigation of safety and privacy
in FoT is beyond the scope of this work.

## Appendix F Complete Experiments for Ablation Studies

### F.1 Effects of Local Reasoning Strategies

From the results in
[Table 20](#A6.T20 "In F.1 Effects of Local Reasoning Strategies ‣ Appendix F Complete Experiments for Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
we see that FoT consistently improves reasoning accuracy and efficiency
under different local reasoning methods, compared to isolated agents
using corresponding local reasoning methods. Complete per-benchmark
accuracies are reported in
[Table 21](#A6.T21 "In F.1 Effects of Local Reasoning Strategies ‣ Appendix F Complete Experiments for Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning").
We tune the hyperparameters of our baselines and report the best average
accuracies we obtain. Lower performance in some baselines does not imply
that these methods are generally ineffective; rather, it suggests that
their mechanisms are less suited to this setting of insight-library
construction. For Agentic Context Engineering
(ACE) \[[44](#bib.bib28)\], we observe a known limitation identified in
prior work \[[44](#bib.bib28)\]: if the Reflector fails to extract
meaningful insights from generated traces or outcomes, the constructed
context may become noisy or even harmful. We set the maximum number of
reflector rounds to 5. On mathematical datasets, ACE generates some
misleading traces, leading to performance drops. FoT, in contrast, can
help mitigate such effects. Evolving Prompts \[[31](#bib.bib29)\] has
known drawbacks in terms of sensitivity to the in-context prompt
template and stability. Despite these limitations, plugging them into
FoT still improves performance.
