### F.2 Effects of Heterogeneous Local and Server Agent Models

We report in
[Table 23](#A6.T23 "In F.2 Effects of Heterogeneous Local and Server Agent Models ‣ Appendix F Complete Experiments for Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
the performance when the local agents are DeepSeek (or Gemini 3.0 Pro)
and the server model is Gemini 3.0 Pro (or DeepSeek), respectively.
Although using DeepSeek as the server for Gemini 3.0 Pro local agents
performs worse than using Gemini 3.0 Pro as the server, it still
outperforms the single-agent baseline.

For the task of research insight discovery, we replace the server agent
from Gemini 2.0 Flash with Gemini 3.0 Pro. The results
[Table 24](#A6.T24 "In F.2 Effects of Heterogeneous Local and Server Agent Models ‣ Appendix F Complete Experiments for Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
confirm our conclusion that a stronger server LLM further improves
performance.

reflecting one potential realistic setting where multiple agents

### F.3 Effects of Insight Library Size

Here, we demonstrate the effects of insight library size on the ML
research insight discovery application. Recall that one baseline is
isolated reasoning, and the other baseline is to query the ML research
insights through a RAG system, where we store old papers in an external
database as reference. In
[Prompt 3](#prompt3 "In G.1 Prompts for Our Instantiation of FoT ‣ Appendix G Complete Prompts ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
we replace the phrase ’proper number’ with explicit quantities (e.g.,
10, 50, 100). From
[Figure 9](#A6.F9 "In F.3 Effects of Insight Library Size ‣ Appendix F Complete Experiments for Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
we can see that as the number of insights increases, the guidance rate
of all three approaches increases, and FoT outperforms the other two. We
note that when FoT does not have strict constraints on the total number
of insights, it will automatically arrive at a good tradeoff between the
number of insights and performance (20), since the performance gain
increases slowly from 20 insights to 200. We can see that RAG can be
effective in encoding external information, but it requires maintenance
of a potentially huge datastore (storing all the previous papers), which
takes more space than a lightweight insight library.

Figure 9: Comparison of FoT, isolated agents, and RAG in their ability
to generate insights that can cover the core contributions of ICLR 2025
papers (guidance rate) under varying numbers of generated insights.
Local agents use Gemini-2.0-Flash as the base LLM and are fed with ICLR
2024 papers as input. FoT generates higher-quality insights that better
guide future research directions while requiring less input text, hence
reducing token consumption.

### F.4 Effects of Agent Participation

Figure 10: Paper guidance rate across different levels of local agent
participation where each agent reads one paper. Guidance rate increases
as participation increases (i.e., more input tasks).

Figure 11: Paper guidance rate across different numbers of total agents,
where the total number of papers read is fixed at 2260. The guidance
rates remain high under different numbers of agents.

We further analyze the impact of varying the number of participating
agents in FoT under two settings. In
[Figure 10](#A6.F10 "In F.4 Effects of Agent Participation ‣ Appendix F Complete Experiments for Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
each agent reads one paper while we vary the total number of papers,
simulating partial participation as in cross-device federated learning.
For each setting with 25%, 50%, and 75% local agents, we repeat the
experiment three times, each with randomly selected papers to mitigate
variation in paper quality. In
[Figure 11](#A6.F11 "In F.4 Effects of Agent Participation ‣ Appendix F Complete Experiments for Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
we fix the total number of papers across agents but vary how many papers
each agent reads before generating reasoning traces. When we use 2,260
agents, each agent generates reasoning traces after reading a single
paper, whereas with 91 agents, each agent generates reasoning traces
after reading 25 papers. We set the max insight library size to 200. For
ICLR 2024 papers, we partition them across agents via primary research
area so that each agent takes as input papers from the same areas. We
observe that the number of agents does not significantly impact
performance. However, assigning all papers to a single agent can result
in an input size that exceeds the model’s context window when performing
local reasoning.
[Table 26](#A6.T26 "In F.4 Effects of Agent Participation ‣ Appendix F Complete Experiments for Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
and
[Table 27](#A6.T27 "In F.4 Effects of Agent Participation ‣ Appendix F Complete Experiments for Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
present the performance on each benchmark for the two experimental
settings in
[Section 6.4](#S6.SS4 "6.4 Effects of Insight Library Size ‣ 6 Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning").
In
[Table 26](#A6.T26 "In F.4 Effects of Agent Participation ‣ Appendix F Complete Experiments for Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
all results except those on the diagonal from the top-left to the
bottom-right correspond to evaluations where the benchmark is not used
during insight library construction, and performance improvements are
observed. In
[Table 27](#A6.T27 "In F.4 Effects of Agent Participation ‣ Appendix F Complete Experiments for Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
the diagonal entries represent cases where the benchmark is not used
during insight library construction, and improvements are also observed.
These results confirm that, in FoT, the insight library can be
effectively used by newly participating agents, as well as by agents
that did not contribute to its construction, to improve performance.

[Table 28](#A6.T28 "In F.4 Effects of Agent Participation ‣ Appendix F Complete Experiments for Ablation Studies ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
compares the costs of the two settings with those of FoT and isolated
agents. The costs of FoT and the two settings include agent inference,
reasoning trace extraction, and server-side aggregation. In the
Include-One setting, creating an insight library requires only about
\$0.15 in additional cost. Once constructed, this library can also
benefit newly participating agents, improving their performance while
reducing inference token usage. Therefore, the benefit of the insight
library is persistent: agents that did not participate in library
construction can still leverage it to achieve higher accuracy, use fewer
tokens, and reduce long-term costs.

## Appendix G Complete Prompts

### G.1 Prompts for Our Instantiation of FoT

[Prompt 1](#prompt1 "In G.1 Prompts for Our Instantiation of FoT ‣ Appendix G Complete Prompts ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
shows the prompt used by agents when an insight library is available. In
[Sections 4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Mathematical Problem Solving ‣ 4 Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Multi-Domain Collaboration ‣ 4 Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
and [4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Research Insight Discovery ‣ 4 Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
we directly apply this prompt to generate responses. In
[Section 4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Real-World Daily Tasks ‣ 4 Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"),
we incorporate this prompt into the OpenClaw system prompt by specifying
that “available insights are stored in insight.md.” When no insight
library is provided (i.e., isolated agents), the prompt reduces to
“Problem: {problem},” where {problem} corresponds to the original
dataset query. We put each problem prompt in
[Section G.2](#A7.SS2 "G.2 Complete Problem Prompts ‣ Appendix G Complete Prompts ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning").

List of Prompts 1 Generating solution

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Available Insights to Guide Your Solution:

{insight library}

---

INSTRUCTIONS: Review the insights above and actively apply the relevant
techniques from insights to solve this problem. Consider which insights
can help you approach the problem more effectively.

Problem: {problem}

[Prompt 2](#prompt2 "In G.1 Prompts for Our Instantiation of FoT ‣ Appendix G Complete Prompts ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
is used for solution reflection, which is the first part of ’Step 2:
Local reasoning and self-reflection’
([Figure 1](#S3.F1 "In 3 Federation over Text ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")),
before an agent generates reasoning traces.

List of Prompts 2 Reflecting on Solution

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Analyze the solution below to extract procedural knowledge that reflects
the reasoning traces.

Problem:

{problem}

Step-by-Step Solution:

{solution}

Your task: Extract the fundamental techniques used in resolution that
can be packaged as reasoning traces. Focus on:

1. What step-by-step procedures were used? How can these be repeated?

2. What conditions determined which approach to use? When should each
   technique apply?

3. What methods, strategies, or workflows can be applied to similar
   problems?

4. What made this approach effective? What should someone know to use it
   correctly?

5. What types of problems would benefit from these techniques?

Output your analysis covering:

\### I. Procedural Knowledge

- Break down the solution into clear, repeatable procedures

- The extracted traces should be concrete solutions rather than general
  principles.

\### II. Reusable Techniques and Methods

- List specific techniques, strategies, or workflows used

- The techniques should be solid on practical questions rather than very
  general and high-level principles.

- For each technique, identify:

\* When it should be used (conditions/triggers)

\* How it was applied (concrete steps)

\* Why it was effective (insights)

\* What problems it could solve (applicability)

\### III. Critical Insights and Guidelines

- What key insights made this solution work?

- What common pitfalls should be avoided?

- What variations or edge cases should be considered?

Focus on extracting actionable, procedural knowledge that can be
packaged as reusable insights for similar problems.

[Prompt 3](#prompt3 "In G.1 Prompts for Our Instantiation of FoT ‣ Appendix G Complete Prompts ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")
is used for the generation of reasoning traces, which is the second part
of ‘Step 2: Local reasoning and self-reflection’
([Figure 1](#S3.F1 "In 3 Federation over Text ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")).
The description includes our definitions of reasoning traces.

List of Prompts 3 Generating Reasoning Trace

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Extract reasoning traces from the solution below. Analyze the solution
and reflection to identify concrete, actionable traces so that similar
problems can be solved via the traces

Problem: {problem}

Solution: {solution}

Reflection: {reflection}

\*\*Your Task:\*\*

Identify and extract all reusable reasoning traces, techniques, and
methods used in the solution. Each trace should be a concrete procedure
that can guide someone to solve similar problems.

\*\*What Makes a Good Reasoning Trace:\*\*

- A specific technique or method that was used in the solution.

- Something that can be applied to similar problems, not just this one.

- Includes guidance on when and how to use it with clear steps that can
  be followed if necessary.

- Not repetition of already well-known or commonly adopted techniques.

- Not too general and high-level but contains actionable procedural
  knowledge.

\*\*Description Must Include:\*\*

1. \*\*Core idea\*\*: The fundamental concept of what this trace is
   about. What is the main technique or method? What does it do?

2. \*\*When to use\*\*: Explain when this skill should be applied. What
   types of problems? What conditions must be met? What situations trigger
   this skill?

\*\*Output Format (Simple JSON):\*\*

Output a simple JSON object with skill names as keys and descriptions as
string values:

{{"trace_name": "description"}}

Format Rules:

- Use valid JSON format

- Each trace name must start with "trace\_"

- Keep JSON simple - no nested objects, just key-value pairs

- Escape quotes in descriptions with backslash: \\"

\*\*Example:\*\*

{{

"trace polynomialFactoring": "The major idea is how we can turn a
polynomial into a product of simpler expressions. This skill is
particularly useful for quadratic and higher-degree polynomial equations
where factoring can simplify the problem. Factoring reduces complex
polynomials to simpler equations. When solving equations with polynomial
expressions that can be factored, especially when the polynomial has
recognizable patterns like difference of squares (a^2-b^2), perfect
square trinomials (a^2+2ab+b^2), or common factors.

"trace depthFirstSearchImplementation": "This algorithm is essential for
problems involving path finding, cycle detection, topological sorting,
connected components, or exploring all possible solutions in a search
space. DFS explores depth before breadth, using stack-based recursion or
explicit stack. It is memory-efficient for deep structures and naturally
handles backtracking. The visited set prevents infinite loops and
redundant work. DFS is the foundation for many graph algorithms
including topological sort, strongly connected components, and maze
solving. When you need to explore or traverse a graph, tree, or nested
structure systematically, going as deep as possible before backtracking.
Use DFS when you need to visit all nodes in a connected component, find
paths between nodes, detect cycles, or explore recursive structures like
file systems, nested data, or game states. "

}}

\*\*Your Task:\*\*

You are extracting fundamental insights from a collection of
problem-solving traces.

\*\*Output Requirements (STRICT):\*\*

6. Every value must be a single string.

7. No nested objects, no nested arrays.

\*\*Required JSON shape:\*\*

{{

"insight_name1": "description string",

"insight_name2": "description string"

}}

\*\*Formatting Rules:\*\*

- Use valid JSON syntax only.

- Keep top-level as key-value pairs only.

- Escape quotes in descriptions with backslash: \\"

- If uncertain, still output a valid JSON object (possibly with fewer
  insights), never free text.

Your goal is to extract a comprehensive set of fundamental, cross-domain
insights that can be derived and applied beyond their original domain
and meet the following requirements:

- Combine previous insights (if any): {existing_encyclopedia if
  existing_encyclopedia else "None"} with new insights.

- Extract your insights based on all client reasoning traces:
  {all_insights_text}. These traces are derived from solving specific
  problems (bottom-up approach)

- Use clusters of reasoning traces: {clusters_text if clusters_text else
  "None identified"} to help organize.

- Use relationships between traces:
  {json.dumps(profiling.get(’relationships’, \[\]), indent=2) if
  isinstance(profiling, dict) else "None identified"} to help organization

- Your task is to extract multi-disciplinary, fundamental knowledge
  (top-down approach) which can be generalized to multi-domain
  problem-solving.

- The extracted insights should be able to DERIVE and GUIDE the use of
  the collected insights

- The extracted insights cannot be too general. They are not supposed to
  be knowledge which can be applied to any problem. They should be
  fundamental knowledge to particular several domains but specific.

- You should extract proper number of insights. Not too few. Not too
  many. Do not over simplify or be too detailed.

- DO NOT over-merge insights.

Insights should have following properties:

1. \*\*Extract Reusable Primitives\*\*:

- For EACH cluster, extract multiple fundamental insights capturing
  core essence and variations (DO NOT over-merge)

- Identify cross-domain patterns that apply to multiple fields

- Create reusable, composable primitives specific enough to be
  actionable

2. \*\*Knowledge to include\*\*:

- \*\*Fundamental Level\*\*: Core principles underlying multiple
  domains

- \*\*General Level\*\*: Broad techniques for related problem types

- \*\*Cross-Domain\*\*: Insights transferable beyond origin field

3. \*\*Preserve While Generalizing\*\*:

- Create fundamental versions that can guide/derive original insights

- Maintain important variations rather than collapsing into single

4. \*\*Description Format:\*\*

Each description is a single string containing:

\*\*Example 1 - Transformer Architecture:\*\*

Input reasoning traces:

- reasoning trace VisionTransformerImageClassification: "I need to
  classify medical X-ray images into disease categories. CNNs aren’t
  working well - they can’t capture relationships between distant regions
  like how fluid in the lower right lung might relate to heart
  enlargement. Let me try Vision Transformer (ViT). I’ll divide each X-ray
  into 16x16 patches - a 224x224 image gives 196 patches. Each patch
  becomes like a token in NLP. I flatten each to a 256-dim vector. Since
  transformers don’t know spatial positions, I add position embeddings so
  the model knows patch \[0,0\] is top-left. I prepend a \[CLS\] token to
  gather global info. Feeding through 12 transformer encoder layers - the
  self-attention lets every patch attend to every other patch directly, so
  patch \[2,5\] can look at patch \[10,12\] even though they’re far apart
  spatially. This is exactly what I need! After 12 layers, I extract the
  \[CLS\] token and feed to MLP classifier. Training on 50k chest X-rays:
  94.2% accuracy, beating ResNet-50’s 89.3%. The attention maps show it’s
  correctly attending to both lungs simultaneously for pneumonia
  detection, linking heart size to lung fluid - this cross-region
  reasoning is what CNNs miss. The key: treating image patches as tokens
  with self-attention enables global spatial reasoning."

- reasoning trace TransformerNextWordPrediction: "I’m building
  autocomplete for a text editor. The challenge: predict next word given
  arbitrary-length context. RNNs struggle with long sequences - the hidden
  state forgets earlier context. Let me use a transformer decoder. I
  tokenize ’The cat sat on the’ using WordPiece -\> tokens \[254, 8901,
  4523, 651, 278\]. Convert each to 512-dim embedding and add positional
  encodings. Critical part: causal masking so the model can’t cheat by
  seeing future words. When predicting token at position 4, it should only
  see 0-3. I implement lower-triangular attention mask. Processing through
  6 decoder layers with masked self-attention. At position 4 (’the’),
  attention computes similarity between its query and keys of previous
  words. It attends strongly to ’sat’ (0.8) and ’on’ (0.7), weakly to
  ’cat’ (0.2). Using 12 heads helps - different heads capture different
  patterns: head-2 learns syntax (preposition+article), head-5 learns
  semantics (actions+objects), head-8 learns long-range dependencies.
  After final layer, project last hidden state through 50k-dim softmax.
  For ’the’: top predictions are ’mat’ (0.73), ’floor’ (0.12), ’rug’
  (0.08). Deployed in production - users accept top-3 suggestion 85\\ of
  the time, reducing typing by 40\\. Transformer’s self-attention captures
  context way better than RNN’s sequential processing."

Output aggregated insight:

{{

"insight_transformerArchitecture": "This fundamental neural network
architecture applies across natural language processing, computer
vision, time series analysis, graph neural networks, and multi-modal
learning. This insight is essential for modern AI applications including
language models, image processing, code generation, and scientific
computing. When you need to capture relationships between all elements
simultaneously (self-attention), you’re working with sequences of
variable length, you need parallel processing of sequences, or when the
problem involves understanding context and relationships. Details: 1)
Design input representation - convert your data into embeddings (token
embeddings for text, patch embeddings for images, node embeddings for
graphs), add positional encodings to preserve sequence information, and
prepare input for transformer blocks 2) Create models with transformer
blocks 3) Apply task-specific architecture - use encoder-only for
understanding (BERT, ViT), decoder-only for generation (GPT), or
encoder-decoder for translation"

}}

\*\*Example 2 - Surface-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy:\*\*

Input reasoning traces:

- reasoning trace SERSMedicalDetectionR6G: "I need to detect cancer
  biomarkers in blood at incredibly low concentrations - 10^-12 M, like
  finding molecules in a swimming pool. ELISA only goes to 10^-9 M, not
  sensitive enough for early diagnosis. Let me try SERS - Surface-Enhanced
  Raman Spectroscopy. Metal nanoparticles create huge EM field
  enhancements. I synthesize 60nm gold nanoparticles via citrate
  reduction. At 785nm laser, these have plasmon resonance amplifying local
  field by ~10^6. But I need selectivity too - can’t detect everything. So
  I functionalize the gold with anti-PSA antibodies for prostate cancer.
  When I add patient serum, only PSA proteins bind. Here’s the clever
  part: I add R6G (Rhodamine 6G) reporter molecules. R6G has enormous
  Raman cross-section and when it sits in nanogaps between gold particles,
  field enhancement shoots to 10^8 or 10^10. Incubate 30 min for PSA
  binding, add R6G which sticks near bound PSA. Hit with 785nm laser at
  5mW - I see characteristic R6G peaks at 1650, 1510, 1310 cm^-1. Peak
  intensity directly proportional to PSA amount. Integrate 60 sec for good
  SNR. Comparing to calibration: detecting PSA at 0.1 ng/mL - that’s
  10,000x more sensitive than ELISA! On clinical samples, detected
  prostate cancer 3-6 months earlier than conventional tests. The
  breakthrough: combining selective antibody recognition with SERS
  amplification gives single-molecule sensitivity while maintaining
  specificity."

- reasoning trace SERSPollutantDetection: "Monitoring river water for
  pesticides. EPA limit for malathion is 0.1 ppb but standard
  chromatography needs 1 ppb minimum. I need 10x better for early warning.
  SERS might work. Instead of spherical particles, I’ll fabricate silver
  nanorod arrays - sharp tips create hotter hotspots than spheres. Using
  oblique angle deposition: 80nm nanorods with 4:1 aspect ratio on
  silicon. Gaps between rods only 5-10nm - perfect for trapping molecules.
  I calculate enhancement should hit 10^10 at 532nm. Collect river water,
  filter through 0.2\\mu m to remove debris and bacteria. Drop 50 \\mu L
  onto nanorod substrate. During 5-min adsorption, pesticide molecules
  diffuse into nanogaps. Small gap means molecules guaranteed in
  enhancement zone (\<10nm from metal). Rinse gently - removes interfering
  organics/salts but leaves adsorbed pesticides. Excite with 532nm at 2mW,
  matching silver plasmon peak. Even at 0.01 ppb malathion, clear peaks at
  1440 cm^-1 (P=S stretch), 1080 cm^-1 (P-O-C), 640 cm^-1 (C-S). Measuring
  1440 peak height vs calibration standards for quantification. Tested 50
  river sites, cross-validated against LC-MS: R^2=0.97 correlation. Best
  part: do this in field with portable Raman - no lab needed. Real-time
  monitoring at 10x below regulatory limits. The nanorod geometry is
  critical - those sharp tips and tight gaps push enhancement to 10^10."

Output aggregated insight:

{{

"insight_surfaceEnhancedRamanSpectroscopy": "This powerful technique
applies across analytical chemistry, materials science, biosensing,
pharmaceutical analysis, environmental monitoring, and forensics. The
technique achieves single-molecule sensitivity (10^6-10^11 enhancement)
while providing molecular structural information through vibrational
fingerprints. When to use: When you need ultra-sensitive detection below
conventional analytical limits, when you want label-free molecular
identification, when analyzing trace contaminants or biomarkers, or when
field-portable real-time analysis is required. Common steps: 1) Prepare
SERS-active substrate - synthesize plasmonic nanostructures (gold/silver
nanoparticles, nanorods, nanostars) optimizing particle size (20-100
nm), shape, and inter-particle spacing (1-10 nm gaps) to maximize
electromagnetic field enhancement at laser wavelength 2) Functionalize
substrate if needed - modify metallic surface with antibodies, aptamers,
or molecular recognition elements for selective analyte binding and
improved specificity 3) Prepare and apply sample - process sample
(filter, dilute, concentrate as needed), deposit onto SERS substrate via
drop-casting or flow-through, allow adsorption time for molecules to
enter hot spots (\<10 nm from metal surface) 4) Select laser
parameters - choose wavelength matching plasmon resonance (532, 633, or
785 nm), optimize power (0.1-10 mW) to avoid sample damage while
maximizing signal 5) Acquire SERS spectrum - collect Raman scattered
light with appropriate integration time, record vibrational spectrum
showing characteristic molecular peaks 6) Analyze spectral fingerprint -
identify molecules by comparing peak positions to reference spectra,
quantify concentration from peak intensities using calibration curves,
assess molecular orientation from peak ratios 7) Validate and control
quality - average multiple spots for reproducibility, use internal
standards, verify with orthogonal methods, consider substrate
heterogeneity and enhancement factor variations"

}}

List of Prompts 6 Judging Whether Paper Contributions Match with the

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

You are evaluating whether a research paper’s proposed solutions are
guided by or directly derived from insights in an encyclopedia.

Insights:

{insights_prompt}

Research Paper:

{paper_text}

Evaluation Criteria - An insight guides the paper ONLY IF ALL of the
following are true:

1. CONCRETE METHODOLOGY USAGE: The insight’s methodology or approach is
   concretely used in the paper’s methods/approach section, not just
   theoretically relevant or mentioned in motivation.

2. METHODS SECTION PRESENCE: The insight must be related to how the
   paper actually implements its solution (methods, algorithms,
   techniques), not just in problem statement or related work.

3. COUNTERFACTUAL TEST: The paper’s core contribution would
   fundamentally differ or fail without this insight. Ask: "If the authors
   didn’t know this insight, could they still arrive at the same core
   solution?"

4. SPECIFICITY: The insight must specifically address a key challenge or
   component of the paper’s solution, not just be generally applicable
   background knowledge.

Response Format:

- Respond ONLY in valid JSON with keys: guided (boolean),
  matched_insights (array of insight names)

- Set guided=true ONLY when at least one insight passes ALL criteria
  above

- Use only exact insight names from the Insights list above

## Appendix H Insights, Raw Reasoning Processes, and Reasoning Traces

### H.1 Representative Insights

In this section, we show example insights. The first three examples is
from the library that are created in the ML research insight discovery
application, derived from ICLR 2023 papers (Setting 1).

With Gemini 3.0 Pro Preview and ICLR 2023 papers, we obtain three
insights: structured output prediction
([Insight 1](#insight1 "In H.1 Representative Insights ‣ Appendix H Insights, Raw Reasoning Processes, and Reasoning Traces ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")),
causal representation learning
([Insight 2](#insight2 "In H.1 Representative Insights ‣ Appendix H Insights, Raw Reasoning Processes, and Reasoning Traces ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")),
and physics-informed deep learning
([Insight 3](#insight3 "In H.1 Representative Insights ‣ Appendix H Insights, Raw Reasoning Processes, and Reasoning Traces ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")),
which provide interesting ideas and instructions on how to approach
related research problems. These topics remain cutting-edge research
questions today.

List of Insights 1 Structured Output Prediction (Setting 1)

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

When to use: When the model output is not a simple class or scalar, but
a complex structured object (e.g., a sequence, a tree, a matching, a
code program) where dependencies between output elements must be
modeled. Step-by-step: 1) Define the output space constraints and
dependencies (e.g., grammar rules, bi-partite matching constraints). 2)
Use autoregressive models (like Transformers) to generate elements
sequentially conditioned on history, or non-autoregressive models with
iterative refinement. 3) Apply structural losses (e.g., connectionist
temporal classification, graph edit distance, optimal transport cost)
rather than simple pointwise error. 4) Use inference techniques like
beam search or constrained decoding to find the most likely valid
structure. Key insights: This covers skills like hierarchical bipartite
matching, permutation equivalent modeling, and program synthesis.

List of Insights 2 Causal Representation Learning (Setting 1)

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

When to use: When building models that must robustly identify
cause-and-effect relationships rather than spurious correlations,
enabling interventions and counterfactual reasoning. Step-by-step: 1)
Model the system using a Structural Causal Model (SCM) or Directed
Acyclic Graph (DAG). 2) Distinguish between invariant causal mechanisms
(stable across environments) and spurious associations. 3) Use
interventions (do-calculus) or environmental diversity to discover the
causal graph. 4) Learn representations that satisfy conditional
independence constraints implied by the causal structure
(disentanglement). 5) Optimize for Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) to
find predictors that are optimal across all interventional
distributions. Key insights: This unifies skills like causal mediation
analysis, front-door prompting, and causal shift diagnosis.

List of Insights 3 Physics Informed Deep Learning (Setting 1)

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

When to use: When modeling physical systems governed by partial
differential equations (PDEs), conservation laws, or geometric
constraints (e.g., fluid dynamics, structural mechanics, climate
modeling) where purely data-driven models violate physical validity or
require excessive data. Use this to integrate physical knowledge
directly into the learning process. Step-by-step: 1) Formulate the
governing physical equations (residuals) of the system (e.g.,
Navier-Stokes, Eikonal equation). 2) Design the neural network to output
the physical state variables (velocity, pressure) given spatiotemporal
coordinates. 3) Compute derivatives of the outputs with respect to
inputs using automatic differentiation (Autograd) to evaluate the PDE
residuals. 4) Construct a composite loss function: Data Loss (fitting
observations) + Physics Loss (minimizing PDE residuals) +
Boundary/Initial Condition Loss. 5) Optionally, use hard constraints
(ansatz) or coordinate transformations to enforce boundary conditions by
construction. Key insights: This guides specific skills like
PDE-constrained latent dynamics, soft contact modeling, and neural
operator learning.

In Setting 2, insights generated by Gemini 2.0 Flash are generally
shorter than those by Gemini 3.0 Pro. However, even without knowledge of
future papers, we still obtain interesting insights such as
neuro-symbolic reasoning
([Insight 4](#insight4 "In H.1 Representative Insights ‣ Appendix H Insights, Raw Reasoning Processes, and Reasoning Traces ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning"))
and parameter-efficient model adaptation
([Insight 5](#insight5 "In H.1 Representative Insights ‣ Appendix H Insights, Raw Reasoning Processes, and Reasoning Traces ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")),
which corresponds to what is currently known as parameter-efficient
fine-tuning. It also produces the zero-to-one capability testing insight
([Insight 6](#insight6 "In H.1 Representative Insights ‣ Appendix H Insights, Raw Reasoning Processes, and Reasoning Traces ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")),
which can be adapted to systems research.

List of Insights 4 Neuro Symbolic Reasoning (Setting 2)

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

When to use: When a problem requires both the perceptual flexibility of
neural networks (handling noisy, unstructured data) and the
precision/interpretability of symbolic logic (handling rules, math,
constraints). Step-by-step: 1) Decompose the system into a Neural Module
(perception/pattern matching) and a Symbolic Module
(reasoning/execution). 2) Design an interface layer: converting neural
outputs into discrete symbols (concepts) or differentiable
approximations (soft logic). 3) Use the Symbolic Module to execute
logical rules, programs, or arithmetic on the extracted symbols. 4)
Train end-to-end (via gradients through soft logic) or separately (via
REINFORCE or supervision) to optimize both perception and reasoning
accuracy. Key insights: This abstracts skills like neuro-symbolic prompt
construction, logic constraint integration, and program synthesis.

List of Insights 5 Parameter Efficient Model Adaptation (Setting 2)

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

When to use: When adapting large pre-trained ’foundation’ models (LLMs,
ViTs) to specific downstream tasks without the computational cost of
full fine-tuning. Step-by-step: 1) Freeze the bulk of the pre-trained
model parameters. 2) Introduce a small set of trainable parameters:
Adapters (bottleneck layers between existing layers), Prompt/Prefix
Tuning (learnable input tokens), or Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA -
decomposing weight updates into low-rank matrices). 3) Train only these
new parameters on the task-specific dataset. 4) Optionally, use
techniques like weight averaging (model soup) or dynamic routing to
combine multiple adaptations. Key insights: This covers skills like
minimalist adapter co-training, prompt engineering, and efficient
fine-tuning protocols.

List of Insights 6 Zero-To-One Capability Testing (Setting 2)

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

When to use: When assessing the functional value of a new technology or
method to distinguish between efficiency gains and capability unlocks.
This applies to product management, feature prioritization, and
evaluating ’breakthrough’ research. Step-by-step: 1) Ignore quantitative
metrics (speed, cost, error rate) initially 2) Define the ’Capability
Boundary’ of the previous state-of-the-art---specifically what tasks it
physically could not perform 3) Ask the binary question: ’Does the new
solution enable a task that was previously impossible/intractable?’ 4)
If the answer is ’No’ (it just does existing tasks better), classify as
’1-to-N’ (Incremental) 5) If the answer is ’Yes’ (it opens a new action
space), classify as ’0-to-1’ (Non-Incremental) 6) Prioritize 0-to-1
capabilities for strategic innovation as they create new markets.

The following examples are drawn from an insight library generated by
Gemini-3.1-Pro under a high-thinking setting on PinchBench. These
examples show that FoT can produce insights that serve as decision
support in areas such as software engineering and market analysis.

List of Insights 7 Declarative Architecture Standardization (PinchBench)

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

This software engineering standard applies modern, declarative
configurations and specific directory layouts to project initialization
to ensure long-term maintainability and out-of-the-box compatibility
with modern build tools. When to use: Whenever initiating, refactoring,
or defining the architecture of new code libraries, packages, or
microservices. Details: 1) Implement the ’src’ layout paradigm (placing
core modules inside a src/ directory adjacent to tests) to force testing
against the installed package version rather than local directory
masking. 2) Utilize declarative metadata configuration files (like
pyproject.toml compliant with PEP 517/518) instead of legacy imperative
scripts (like setup.py) to manage dependencies and build instructions.

List of Insights 8 Differentiator Focused Market Deconstruction
(PinchBench)

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

This competitive intelligence framework distills crowded market
landscapes into highly actionable artifacts by ignoring parity and
focusing exclusively on divergence. When to use: When conducting tech
stack evaluations, vendor selections, or business intelligence reporting
in mature industries where competitors share a massive baseline of
identical functionalities. Details: 1) Scan macro industry trends before
drilling into micro profiles. 2) Explicitly identify and filter out
industry-standard baseline features (’table stakes’). 3) Abstract highly
volatile data (like exact dollar costs) into broader operational
paradigms. 4) Integrate recent structural context like M&A
parent-company ownership. 5) Map the remaining unique architectural
roots and target audience differences onto a structured
cross-dimensional comparison matrix.

List of Insights 9 UI Bypass File Routing (PinchBench)

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

This fundamental operational pattern separates back-end automated
artifacts from front-end conversational interfaces. It solves the
’double print’ token clutter problem by writing generated payloads
directly to the file system while returning only a synthesized ’Bottom
Line Up Front’ (BLUF) or status summary to the user interface. When to
use: Apply this whenever executing tasks that generate large artifacts
(codebases, CSVs, long-form reports) or orchestrate closed-loop file
transformations (read-process-write), specifically when the user
provides explicit destination commands like ’Save to’ or ’Create a
file’. Details: 1) Generate the primary payload internally. 2) Pipe
payload via a file-write tool directly to persistent storage. 3) Verify
successful byte-count written. 4) Output only a brief executive summary
confirming completion and detailing core contents.

### H.2 Complete Raw Reasoning Process for Case Studies in [Section D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Multi-Domain Collaboration ‣ Appendix D Complete Experiments for Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")

List of Reasoning Processes 1 Incorrect Reasoning Process of GPQA
Diamond Problem 89 (Round 2)

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Solution Response: \*\*Step-by-Step Analysis:\*\*

1. \*\*Analysis of Product 1 Formation:\*\*

\* Starting Material: 1,3-dibromoadamantane.

\* Reagents: KOH, 240C.

\* This reaction is a known Grob-type fragmentation of the adamantane
skeleton. The 1,3-functionalization allows for the cleavage of a C-C
bond in the cage, leading to a bicyclic system.

\* The spectral data for Product 1 confirms this:

\* IR 1720 cm\$^{-1}\$ indicates a ketone (\$C=O\$).

\* \${}^1\$H NMR 4.79 ppm (2H) indicates terminal vinylic protons
(\$=CH_2\$), which typically appear in the 4.5-5.0 ppm range.

\* The structure consistent with this data and the starting material is
\*\*3-methylenebicyclo\[3.3.1\]nonan-7-one\*\* (or
7-methylenebicyclo\[3.3.1\]nonan-3-one due to symmetry). This molecule
has the formula \$C\_{10}H\_{14}O\$ and fits the unsaturation index.

2. \*\*Analysis of Product 2 Formation:\*\*

\* Reagents: Product 1 + Excess Aluminum Isopropoxide
(\$Al(OiPr)\_3\$) + Heat.

\* This is the \*\*Meerwein-Ponndorf-Verley (MPV) reduction\*\*. It
selectively reduces ketones to alcohols.

\* \*\*Stereochemistry:\*\* The MPV reduction is reversible and, under
heated conditions with excess reagent, typically yields the
\*\*thermodynamic product\*\*.

\* In the bicyclo\[3.3.1\]nonane system, substituents at positions 3 and
7 face severe transannular steric repulsion if they are in the
\*\*endo\*\* (equatorial-like pointing inwards) position. Therefore, the
stable conformer places bulky groups in the \*\*exo\*\* (axial-like
pointing outwards) position.

\* Consequently, the thermodynamic product of the reduction is the
\*\*exo-alcohol\*\* (where the OH group is axial).

\* Product 2 is \*\*exo-3-methylenebicyclo\[3.3.1\]nonan-7-ol\*\*.

3. \*\*Analysis of Product 3 Formation:\*\*

\* Reagents: Product 2 + Ozone (\$O_3\$), -78C, followed by DMS.

\* This is an \*\*ozonolysis\*\* reaction with reductive workup. It
cleaves the exocyclic carbon-carbon double bond (\$=CH_2\$) and converts
it into a carbonyl group (\$C=O\$).

\* The stereocenter at C7 (bearing the OH group) is unaffected.

\* Product 3 is \*\*exo-7-hydroxybicyclo\[3.3.1\]nonan-3-one\*\*.

4. \*\*NMR Prediction for Product 3:\*\*

\* \*\*Target Proton:\*\* The question asks for the coupling pattern of
the "most deshielded hydrogen atom" (excluding exchangeable OH).

\* In Product 3, the proton on the carbon bearing the hydroxyl group
(H-C7) is the most deshielded due to the electronegativity of oxygen
(chemical shift typically 3.5 - 4.5 ppm).

\* \*\*Stereochemistry of H-C7:\*\* Since the hydroxyl group (OH) is in
the \*\*exo (axial)\*\* position (thermodynamic product), the geminal
hydrogen atom (H-C7) must be in the \*\*endo (equatorial)\*\* position.

\* \*\*Coupling Analysis:\*\*

\* The H-C7 (equatorial) proton is coupled to four vicinal protons on
the adjacent bridge carbons (C6 and C8).

\* Due to the molecular symmetry (plane passing through C3-C7-C9), the
protons on C6 are equivalent to those on C8.

\* The neighbors are: H-6ax, H-6eq, H-8ax, H-8eq.

\* Coupling constants for an equatorial proton in a chair-like ring are
generally small: \$J\_{eq-ax} \\approx 2-5\$ Hz and \$J\_{eq-eq}
\\approx 2-5\$ Hz.

\* Because the coupling constants are small and of similar magnitude,
the splitting pattern typically appears as a \*\*pentet\*\* (quintet)
(representing overlap of couplings to 4 protons).

\* (Note: If the H were axial, it would show large trans-diaxial
couplings (~10-12 Hz) and small axial-equatorial couplings, resulting in
a distinct triplet of triplets. Since we have the thermodynamic
exo-alcohol, the H is equatorial, ruling out the triplet of triplets).

\*\*Conclusion:\*\* The most deshielded hydrogen is the equatorial H at
C7, which couples to four neighbors with similar small coupling
constants, producing a pentet.

\\boxed{D}

List of Reasoning Processes 2 Correct Reasoning Process of GPQA Diamond
Problem 89 (Round 3)

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Solution Response: \*\*Step 1: Structure Elucidation of Product 1\*\*

The starting material is 1,3-dibromoadamantane. Heating this with excess
KOH at high temperatures (\$240^\\circ\\text{C}\$) is a known
fragmentation reaction involving the adamantane skeleton. The conditions
facilitate a Grob-type fragmentation of the 1,3-functionalized system to
form a bicyclic compound. The data provided for Product 1 supports this:

\* \*\*IR 1720 cm\$^{-1}\$\*\*: Indicates a ketone (C=O).

\* \*\*\$^{1}\\text{H}\$ NMR\*\*: The signal at \$\\delta 4.79\$ (2H)
corresponds to an exocyclic methylene group (\$=\\text{CH}\_2\$). The
remaining protons (12H) fit the bicyclic skeleton.

The structure formed is \*\*7-methylenebicyclo\[3.3.1\]nonan-3-one\*\*.
This molecule fits the formula (\$C\_{10}H\_{14}O\$) and the spectral
data.

\*\*Step 2: Structure Elucidation of Product 2\*\*

Product 1 is heated with excess aluminum isopropoxide. These are the
conditions for a \*\*Meerwein-Ponndorf-Verley (MPV) reduction\*\*.

\* The MPV reduction converts the ketone at C3 to a secondary alcohol.

\* Crucially, MPV reductions are reversible and thermodynamically
controlled, yielding the more stable alcohol isomer.

\* In 3-substituted bicyclo\[3.3.1\]nonanes, the \*\*exo-isomer\*\*
(substituent in the equatorial position) is thermodynamically more
stable than the endo-isomer (substituent in the axial position). This is
because the endo position suffers from severe transannular steric
repulsion with the C7 position (even with the change in hybridization at
C7, the exo-alcohol remains the preferred thermodynamic product in these
systems).

\* Therefore, Product 2 is
\*\*exo-7-methylenebicyclo\[3.3.1\]nonan-3-ol\*\*.

\* Stereochemistry: The hydroxyl group is \*\*exo (equatorial)\*\*.
Consequently, the carbinol hydrogen atom (H-3) is \*\*endo (axial)\*\*.

\*\*Step 3: Structure Elucidation of Product 3\*\*

Product 2 is subjected to ozonolysis (\$O_3\$, then \$Me_2S\$).

\* Ozonolysis cleaves the exocyclic carbon-carbon double bond
(\$=\\text{CH}\_2\$) at C7 to form a ketone (\$C=O\$).

\* The alcohol at C3 is unaffected.

\* Product 3 is \*\*exo-7-hydroxybicyclo\[3.3.1\]nonan-3-one\*\* (also
named exo-3-hydroxybicyclo\[3.3.1\]nonan-7-one due to symmetry).

\*\*Step 4: Analysis of the Target Proton\*\*

The question asks for the coupling pattern of the "most deshielded
hydrogen atom" in Product 3.

\* The protons in the molecule are:

\* Protons alpha to the ketone (C2/C4 or C6/C8): \$\\delta \\approx
2.4\$ ppm.

\* Bridgehead protons (C1/C5): \$\\delta \\approx 2.0\$ ppm.

\* Bridge protons (C9): \$\\delta \\approx 1.8\$ ppm.

\* Carbinol proton (H-3, alpha to -OH): \$\\delta \\approx
3.8\\text{--}4.2\$ ppm.

\* The \*\*carbinol proton (H-3)\*\* is the most deshielded
non-exchangeable proton due to the electronegativity of the oxygen atom.

\*\*Step 5: Determining the Coupling Pattern\*\*

We have established that the hydroxyl group is \*\*exo (equatorial)\*\*,
placing the target hydrogen atom (H-3) in the \*\*axial\*\* position of
the cyclohexane-like chair ring.

\* \*\*Neighbors\*\*: The C3 carbon is flanked by two methylene groups
(C2 and C4). Due to the plane of symmetry in the molecule, C2 and C4 are
equivalent.

\* \*\*Coupling Partners\*\*: The axial H-3 couples with:

\* Two \*\*axial\*\* protons (H-2ax, H-4ax).

\* Two \*\*equatorial\*\* protons (H-2eq, H-4eq).

\* \*\*Coupling Constants (\$J\$)\*\*:

\* Axial-Axial coupling (\$J\_{aa}\$) is large, typically 10-12 Hz
(anti-periplanar arrangement).

\* Axial-Equatorial coupling (\$J\_{ae}\$) is small to medium, typically
2-5 Hz (gauche arrangement).

\* \*\*Pattern\*\*:

\* The splitting by the two equivalent large couplings (\$J\_{aa}\$)
creates a triplet (\$1:2:1\$).

\* Each line of this triplet is further split into a triplet by the two
equivalent small couplings (\$J\_{ae}\$).

\* The resulting pattern is a large triplet of small triplets, known as
a \*\*triplet of triplets\*\* (tt).

In contrast, an equatorial proton (which would result from the kinetic
endo-alcohol) typically shows small couplings to all neighbors,
appearing as a pentet or broad multiplet. Since we have the
thermodynamic product (axial H), the answer is the triplet of triplets.

\\boxed{C}

List of Reasoning Processes 3 Incorrect Reasoning Process of AIME25
Problem 28 (Round 1)

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Solution Response: Let the sequence be defined by \$x_1 =
\\frac{25}{11}\$ and \$x\_{k+1} = \\frac{1}{3}\\left(x_k +
\\frac{1}{x_k} - 1\\right)\$.

This simplifies to \$x\_{k+1} = \\frac{x_k^2 - x_k + 1}{3x_k}\$.

Let \$x_k = \\frac{m_k}{n_k}\$ with \$\\gcd(m_k, n_k) = 1\$. Then

\\ x\_{k+1} = \\frac{m_k^2 - m_k n_k + n_k^2}{3m_k n_k}. \\

Let \$m\_{k+1}’ = m_k^2 - m_k n_k + n_k^2\$ and \$n\_{k+1}’ = 3m_k
n_k\$.

The sum of numerator and denominator is \$S\_{k+1}’ = m\_{k+1}’ +
n\_{k+1}’ = m_k^2 + 2m_k n_k + n_k^2 = (m_k + n_k)^2 = S_k^2\$.

The actual terms \$m\_{k+1}, n\_{k+1}\$ are obtained by dividing by
\$g_k = \\gcd(m\_{k+1}’, n\_{k+1}’)\$.

We have \$\\gcd(m_k^2 - m_k n_k + n_k^2, m_k n_k) = 1\$ since
\$\\gcd(m_k, n_k) = 1\$.

Thus \$g_k = \\gcd((m_k+n_k)^2, 3)\$.

Since \$S_1 = 25+11=36\$, which is divisible by 3, we have \$g_1 = 3\$.

Also, \$S\_{k+1} = S_k^2 / g_k\$. If \$S_k\$ is divisible by 3, then
\$S_k^2\$ is divisible by 9, so \$S\_{k+1} = S_k^2/3\$ is divisible by 3.

Thus by induction, \$g_k=3\$ for all \$k\$, and \$S\_{k+1} = S_k^2 /
3\$.

Let \$T_k = S_k/3\$. Then \$3 T\_{k+1} = (3 T_k)^2 / 3 = 3 T_k^2
\\implies T\_{k+1} = T_k^2\$.

We have \$S_1 = 36\$, so \$T_1 = 12\$.

Then \$T_k = 12^{2^{k-1}}\$, and \$S_k = 3 \\cdot 12^{2^{k-1}}\$.

We need \$S\_{2025} = 3 \\cdot 12^{2^{2024}} \\pmod{1000}\$.

Modulo 8: \$S\_{2025} = 3 \\cdot 4^{2^{2024}} \\cdot 3^{2^{2024}}
\\equiv 0 \\pmod 8\$ (for large exponent).

Modulo 125: \$\\phi(125) = 100\$. The exponent is \$E = 2^{2024}\$.

\$2^{2024} \\equiv 16 \\pmod{100}\$.

So \$S\_{2025} \\equiv 3 \\cdot 12^{16} \\pmod{125}\$.

\$12^{16} \\equiv 84 \\pmod{125}\$.

\$S\_{2025} \\equiv 3 \\cdot 84 = 252 \\equiv 2 \\pmod{125}\$.

We solve the system \$x \\equiv 0 \\pmod 8\$ and \$x \\equiv 2
\\pmod{125}\$.

\$x = 125k + 2\$. \$125k + 2 \\equiv 5k + 2 \\equiv 0 \\pmod 8 \\implies
5k \\equiv -2 \\equiv 6 \\implies k \\equiv 6 \\pmod 8\$.

\$x = 125(6) + 2 = 750 + 2 = 752\$.

\\boxed{752}

List of Reasoning Processes 4 Correct Reasoning Process of AIME25
Problem 28 (Round 2)

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Solution Response: To solve for \$x\_{2025}\$, we first analyze the
recurrence relation
\$x\_{k+1}=\\frac{1}{3}\\left(x_k+\\frac{1}{x_k}-1\\right) =
\\frac{x_k^2 - x_k + 1}{3x_k}\$.

Let’s find the fixed points of the transformation \$f(x) = \\frac{x^2 -
x + 1}{3x}\$.

Setting \$f(x) = x\$, we get \$x^2 - x + 1 = 3x^2\$, which implies
\$2x^2 + x - 1 = 0\$. Factoring gives \$(2x-1)(x+1) = 0\$. The fixed
points are \$x = 1/2\$ and \$x = -1\$.

This suggests using a linear fractional transformation that maps these
fixed points to \$0\$ and \$\\infty\$ to simplify the recurrence. Let
\$z_k = \\frac{x_k - 1/2}{x_k + 1} = \\frac{2x_k - 1}{2(x_k + 1)}\$. To
avoid the factor of 2 in the denominator, let’s define \$z_k =
\\frac{2x_k - 1}{x_k + 1}\$.

Let’s find the recurrence for \$z_k\$:

\$\$z\_{k+1} = \\frac{2x\_{k+1} - 1}{x\_{k+1} + 1} =
\\frac{2\\left(\\frac{x_k^2 - x_k + 1}{3x_k}\\right) - 1}{\\frac{x_k^2 -
x_k + 1}{3x_k} + 1} = \\frac{2(x_k^2 - x_k + 1) - 3x_k}{x_k^2 - x_k +
1 + 3x_k} = \\frac{2x_k^2 - 5x_k + 2}{x_k^2 + 2x_k + 1}\$\$

\$\$z\_{k+1} = \\frac{(2x_k - 1)(x_k - 2)}{(x_k + 1)^2} =
\\left(\\frac{2x_k - 1}{x_k + 1}\\right) \\frac{x_k - 2}{x_k + 1}\$\$

We can express \$\\frac{x_k - 2}{x_k + 1}\$ in terms of \$z_k\$. From
\$z_k = \\frac{2x_k - 1}{x_k + 1} = \\frac{2(x_k+1) - 3}{x_k+1} = 2 -
\\frac{3}{x_k+1}\$, we have \$\\frac{3}{x_k+1} = 2 - z_k\$.

Then \$\\frac{x_k - 2}{x_k + 1} = \\frac{x_k + 1 - 3}{x_k + 1} = 1 -
\\frac{3}{x_k+1} = 1 - (2 - z_k) = z_k - 1\$.

Substituting this back, we get:

\$\$z\_{k+1} = z_k (z_k - 1)\$\$

We calculate the first term \$z_1\$:

\$\$x_1 = \\frac{25}{11} \\implies z_1 = \\frac{2(25/11) - 1}{25/11 + 1}
= \\frac{50/11 - 11/11}{25/11 + 11/11} = \\frac{39}{36} =
\\frac{13}{12}\$\$

We can represent \$z_k\$ as a fraction \$N_k/D_k\$.

\$z_1 = \\frac{13}{12}\$.

\$z_2 = \\frac{13}{12} \\left(\\frac{13}{12} - 1\\right) =
\\frac{13}{144}\$.

\$z_3 = \\frac{13}{144} \\left(\\frac{13}{144} - 1\\right) = \\frac{13
\\cdot (-131)}{144^2}\$.

The denominator of \$z_k\$ follows the pattern \$D_k = 12^{2^{k-1}}\$.

The numerator \$N_k\$ and denominator \$D_k\$ are relatively prime (as
derived in the thought process).

We need \$x\_{2025} = \\frac{m}{n}\$. Inverting the transformation \$z =
\\frac{2x-1}{x+1}\$:

\$\$z(x+1) = 2x - 1 \\implies zx + z = 2x - 1 \\implies 1 + z = x(2 - z)
\\implies x = \\frac{1+z}{2-z}\$\$

Substituting \$z\_{2025} = \\frac{N}{D}\$:

\$\$x\_{2025} = \\frac{1 + N/D}{2 - N/D} = \\frac{D + N}{2D - N}\$\$

Since \$\\gcd(N, D) = 1\$ and \$N \\equiv 1 \\pmod 3\$, \$D \\equiv 0
\\pmod 3\$, the fraction is irreducible.

Thus \$m = D + N\$ and \$n = 2D - N\$.

The sum \$m+n = (D+N) + (2D-N) = 3D\$.

We need to calculate \$3D\_{2025} \\pmod{1000}\$.

\$D\_{2025} = 12^{2^{2024}}\$. Let \$E = 2^{2024}\$. We need \$3 \\cdot
12^E \\pmod{1000}\$.

By Chinese Remainder Theorem on \$1000 = 8 \\times 125\$:

1. \*\*Mod 8\*\*: \$12 \\equiv 4 \\pmod 8\$. \$12^E = 4^E\$. Since \$E
   \\ge 2\$, \$4^E\$ is divisible by \$16\$, so \$12^E \\equiv 0 \\pmod
   8\$. Thus \$3 \\cdot 12^E \\equiv 0 \\pmod 8\$.

2. \*\*Mod 125\*\*: We need \$3 \\cdot 12^E \\pmod{125}\$.

Compute \$E \\pmod{\\phi(125)}\$. \$\\phi(125) = 100\$.

\$E = 2^{2024}\$.

\$E \\equiv 0 \\pmod 4\$.

\$E \\pmod{25}\$: \$\\phi(25) = 20\$. \$2024 = 20 \\times 101 + 4\$. \$E
\\equiv 2^4 = 16 \\pmod{25}\$.

Using CRT for mod 100: \$x \\equiv 0 \\pmod 4\$ and \$x \\equiv 16
\\pmod{25}\$ implies \$x \\equiv 16 \\pmod{100}\$.

So we need \$12^{16} \\pmod{125}\$.

\$12^2 = 144 \\equiv 19\$.

\$12^4 \\equiv 19^2 = 361 \\equiv 111 \\equiv -14\$.

\$12^8 \\equiv (-14)^2 = 196 \\equiv 71\$.

\$12^{16} \\equiv 71^2 = 5041 = 40 \\times 125 + 41 \\equiv 41\$.

So \$3 \\cdot 12^E \\equiv 3 \\cdot 41 = 123 \\pmod{125}\$.

Solving for \$X \\equiv 0 \\pmod 8\$ and \$X \\equiv 123 \\pmod{125}\$:

\$X = 125k + 123\$.

\$125k + 123 \\equiv 5k + 3 \\equiv 0 \\pmod 8 \\implies 5k \\equiv -3
\\equiv 5 \\implies k \\equiv 1 \\pmod 8\$.

\$X = 125(1) + 123 = 248\$.

The remainder is 248.

\\boxed{248}

### H.3 Example Reasoning Traces in [Section 4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Research Insight Discovery ‣ 4 Applications of FoT ‣ Federation over Text: Insight Sharing for Multi-Agent Reasoning")

List of Reasoning Traces 1 Inverse Frequency Balancing

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

This method flattens long-tailed (Zipfian) data distributions to prevent
models from overfitting to common ’head’ concepts while underfitting
rare ’tail’ concepts. It uses a probabilistic sampling approach based on
a maximum frequency threshold to ensure a more uniform distribution of
concepts. When to use: When training foundation models or classifiers on
natural data distributions where a small number of classes or concepts
dominate the dataset (e.g., millions of ’cat’ images vs. few ’specific
species’), and the goal is to maximize zero-shot generalization or
task-agnostic performance. Step-by-step: 1) Scan the dataset to
calculate the total count (\$N\$) for every specific metadata concept or
class 2) Define a saturation threshold (\$t\$) that represents the
desired maximum number of samples per concept (e.g., \$t=20,000\$ was
used for 400M total items) 3) Compute a sampling probability for each
concept using the formula \$P = \\min(1, t/N)\$, ensuring tail concepts
are kept with probability 1 and head concepts are downsampled 4) Iterate
through the data points again; for items associated with multiple
concepts, generate a random number against the probability of each
associated concept 5) Select the data point for the final training set
if \*at least one\* of its associated concepts triggers a selection,
thereby preserving diversity even within common items.

List of Reasoning Traces 2 Directional Skill Evolution

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

This technique involves systematically transforming specific, verified
solutions into more general and reusable tools (skills) to enrich a
knowledge base. Instead of just storing a specific answer, the system
actively ’evolves’ it to cover broader cases. When to use: When building
a knowledge base or skill library from specific examples, particularly
in domains like mathematics or coding where a specific solution (e.g.,
for 2D vectors) often hints at a general principle (e.g., for
N-dimensions). It is used to proactively expand the capabilities of an
AI agent without requiring new external problem sets. Step-by-step: 1)
Select a specific, verified skill or lemma from the existing library
(the seed) 2) Choose one of four specific evolution heuristics:
’Parameterize’ (replace specific constants like numbers with variables),
’Extend Dimensions’ (generalize from specific dimensions to
n-dimensions), ’Scale Complexity’ (create a more complex version of the
problem), or ’Identify Key Concepts’ (extract and formalize the core
underlying principle) 3) Retrieve relevant unsolved problems or requests
to guide the evolution context, ensuring the new skill aims at actual
gaps 4) Prompt the model to rewrite the seed skill according to the
chosen heuristic 5) Formally verify the generated skill; if valid and
distinct from existing skills, add it to the library.
